subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING IMPORT SURCHARGES

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter L. Gordon (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF LEGISLATION RESPECTING IMPORT SURCHARGES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a brief statement respecting the surcharge on imports order that was passed by the previous government on June 24, 1962. As hon. members know the legality of this order has been challenged, and the matter is before the courts.
This poses a difficult problem because in many cases those who paid the surcharges, and who might now be entitled to claim refunds should the order be found to have been invalid, passed the amount of such surcharges on to their customers. These customers in turn may have passed the amount of the surcharges on to their customers, and so on. It would not be possible to unscramble a situation of this kind.
Accordingly I should like to inform the house that the government will be recommending legislation on the surcharge order. One effect of this proposed legislation would be to prevent any massive attempt at obtaining refund of moneys in fact paid by now unidentifiable Canadians, an action which would not be in the public interest.

speechtext: The house resumed, from Monday, May 20, consideration of the motion of Miss Pauline Jewett for an address to His Excellency the Governor General in reply to the speech from the throne delivered by His Excellency the Administrator at the opening of the session, and the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefen-baker.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night I was dealing with some of the more glaring omissions from the throne speech. I said that in the light of those omissions, and in the light of the number of questions to which the government in the last two or three days has answered that government policy would be announced in due course, I hope that the 60 days of decision are not to be replaced by 60 weeks of indecision.
The government cannot be allowed, and
must not be allowed, to dawdle. It is in a position in which it must either perform or perish. Earlier in my remarks I said that the opposition groups have a responsibility not to indulge in frivolous obstruction, and that the government in turn has a responsibility to tackle aggressively the problems facing the country and to consult parliament on major policies.
Mr. Speaker, I want to place before the house my contention that the government has already shown a callous disregard of parliament and parliamentary institutions. What is the role of the executive in relation to parliament, and particularly the role of a minority government in relation to parliament? I cannot give the house any better statement than to quote from the speech made by the leader of the Liberal party, addressing a meeting of Liberal M.P.'s and their supporters in the metropolitan area of Toronto on September 18, 1962. This is not taken from a press report but from the press release actually issued by the office of the leader of the Liberal party. At that time the present Prime Minister said:
The other aspect of the election to which I wish to draw special attention is the complete contempt of parliament shown by the Prime Minister since he was left as the head of a minority government; and this by the man who cannot make a speech without boasting how he has restored the rights of parliament.
Responsible government, which was not gained in Canada without bloodshed, is the foundation of our independence and our democracy in this country.
What do we mean by responsible government? We mean that the Queen's ministers are responsible to the elected house of parliament. They have the

right to remain in office only so long as they have the confidence and support of a majority of the elected representatives of the people.
In a parliament where no political party has a clear majority, this confidence cannot, of course, be taken for granted by the government.
The first such parliament in our times was the one elected in October, 1925. At that time Mr. Mackenzie King decided to remain at the head of a minority government until parliament could meet and decide whether or not his government should continue in office. But, and this is in strong contrast to the conduct of the present Prime Minister, Mr. King's government made no appointments and took no action beyond that required for the day-today routine business of government until parliament had met and decided the question of confidence.
The leader of the Liberal party went on:
As soon as it met the acting prime minister, as leader of the government in the house, sought at once to get a vote of confidence without even waiting for action by the opposition. After a very lengthy debate the government was sustained by a vote of 123 to 120. The essential point is that the Liberal government of that time did not presume to do more than to act as a caretaker government until the ministers were assured of a majority in parliament, and took steps to decide that point at the earliest possible moment.
The statement goes on:
I insist that nothing should be done in this parliament or by this parliament until the question of confidence has been settled in the proper constitutional way.
Unless that question is settled first, the right of parliament to control the executive will have ceased to mean anything. No plea of urgency and no excuse should be accepted by the elected representatives of the people, for any further delay in settling the question as to whether or not the Diefenbaker government possesses the confidence and has the support of a majority in the new House of Commons.
I agree with that statement. If the leader of the Liberal party meant it, then it is a ringing declaration of faith in parliamentary government. If he did not mean it, then it is nothing more than hypocritical claptrap, and only time will place this statement in its true perspective.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that the Prime Minister and his colleagues have not made a very good start in this direction. I refer to two matters. First of all I refer to the announcement by the Minister of Fisheries and the Secretary of State for External Affairs that they have decided to accept two recommendations by the international north Pacific fisheries commission to permit Japan to fish for halibut in the east Bering sea and for herring off the Queen Charlotte islands. Apart altogether from the merits of the case, surely it would have been proper to have allowed this house and the fisheries committee of the house to go into this matter and express an opinion. Surely the request of the fishermen involved that they be allowed to make representations to the House
The Address-Mr. Douglas of Commons committee on marine and fisheries was not unreasonable. What was the hurry? I think we have a right to know.
Does the government intend to deal with this matter by an order in council, a minute of cabinet or an executive order, or does it intend to refer this matter to parliament? If it intends to refer it to parliament, then why has a decision been made before parliament has had any opportunity to express its opinion?
An even more glaring example of this disregard of parliament is the government's announced decision to acquire nuclear arms for Canadian forces in Canada and Canadian forces in NATO. In this connection I refer to the speech from the throne, where it says:
For this purpose, the armed forces of Canada should have available the modern weapons necessary to perform effectively the defensive tasks which Canada has undertaken in the alliance.
In this context modern weapons can only be interpreted as referring to nuclear arms. Therefore I wish to move a subamendment.
We cannot support the amendment proposed by the leader of the Conservative party. There are two statements in particular in that amendment, one of which speaks of Canada's economic growth during 1962 as exceeding that of any country in the western world. I would challenge that statement on the basis of growth in terms of constant dollars, taking into consideration price changes. Certainly countries in western Europe with more pronounced economic growth and with unemployment of less than 2 per cent could hardly be said to have had less economic growth and stability than Canada.
I also refer to the last phrase, "to give the people of Canada full opportunity to continue the social advances and economic growth of the past year". I would point out that these social advances and economic growth still left over 500,000 unemployed in this country and large areas of our population with a very low standard of living. Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge):
That the amendment be amended by deleting therefrom all the words after the word "address" and by substituting therefor the following words:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have indicated their intention of acquiring nuclear arms for Canadian forces, thereby lessening the chances for nuclear disarmament and increasing the danger of nuclear war.
Mr. Speaker, I should like to say a few words as to how the government have dealt with this matter since they took office on April 22. Within a few hours of being sworn in the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) announced on television that nuclear

The Address-Mr. Douglas arms would be acquired for Canadian forces in Canada within six weeks, and for NATO forces in Europe within six months.

Prime Minister Pearson said today Canada's acquisition of nuclear weapons did not require formal parliamentary approval.

When was this commitment made, Mr. Speaker? The strange thing is that neither the leader of the Liberal party nor any of his supporters seemed to be aware of this commitment prior to January 12 last, when the leader of the Liberal party changed the party's policy in this respect. I have here the Saskatoon Star-Phoenix of November 29, 1962. Mr. Pearson was speaking to the University of Saskatchewan students, and this report says:

I have no right to deny the Prime Minister the privilege of changing his mind, but I deny him the right to impute motives to those who support the position which he abandoned only a few weeks ago. By whom was this commitment made? It was certainly not made by the government that was in office at that time. They said they had made no such commitment. Certainly parliament made no such commitment. By whom was the commitment made? It is true there were arrangements between the Department of National Defence of this country and the department of defence of the United States. Mr. Speaker, I suggest that no commitment can be made on behalf of this nation except by this parliament, the elected representatives of the people.
I can recall that only a few months ago Liberal members in this house excoriated the government of that day for imposing $250 million worth of surcharges without the approval of parliament. I agreed with them. But I submit, Mr. Speaker, that surely imposing nuclear weapons is a much more serious matter than imposing surcharges, and I contend that if taxation without representation is undemocratic, then annihilation without representation is tyranny.
The government of this country has no clearcut mandate to impose nuclear weapons on this country. Only this parliament can give them that mandate. We in the New Democratic party believe that the acquisition of nuclear arms by Canada will increase the danger of nuclear war and will lessen the chances of nuclear disarmament. We contend that this is a fateful decision which is being

made, and that this decision cannot and must not be made without being referred to this parliament. We believe that the members of this house should have an opportunity to state in clear and categorical terms whether or not Canada should acquire nuclear weapons at home or abroad.
For that reason, Mr. Speaker, I have moved this subamendment, in order that the house may have an opportunity to tell the government exactly where it stands on the matter of nuclear arms. In so far as this party is concerned, our position is unchanged. We believe that acquiring nuclear arms will add nothing to the military security of Canada. It will add nothing to the effectiveness of the NATO alliance. We believe that, on the contrary, it is a retrograde step; that at a time when the foreign secretary of the United Kingdom has made an appeal to the Soviet union not to extend nuclear arms to other countries which do not possess them, Canada might well set an example by saying that as far as we are concerned we intend to keep this country out of the nuclear club.

Mr. Speaker, may I join in the numerous congratulations which you certainly must have received on election to your present office. May I also extend my congratulations to the mover and seconder of the address. The trepidation they must have felt on making their maiden speeches in the house is certainly shared by myself at this moment.
Many of the members on this side of the house-I am referring especially to the newer members-have had backgrounds in academic circles and in the public service which make us proud to be associated with them. They will undoubtedly contribute a great deal to debate in this parliament and to public life in Canada.
The constituency which I have the honour to represent is one of the ten largest in Canada, and for 96 years it maintained its allegiance to one political party. I do not think the voters of Carleton can be accused of contributing to splinter parties in a house of minorities, to use a phrase which I believe the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) used yesterday. They do not lightly change their allegiance, but this riding has undergone profound changes, especially in the post-war period. It now includes a substantial portion of the national capital region and the city of Ottawa in addition to a large rural and agricultural area. In Carle-ton there are no strictly rural interests or strictly urban interests; one blends into the other. We depend upon each other. It will be my privilege to serve all the residents of this riding, both old and new. It has been
The Address-Mr. Francis represented in this house by many distinguished men who rose to high positions, including Sir John A. Macdonald and Sir Robert Borden. It is a great honour to succeed them.
One of the matters concerning which legislation is to be placed before this house, as indicated in the statement of the administrator, is the redistribution of electoral boundaries. I hope it will be possible to agree upon action in this field early in the session. Generally speaking, the people in our cities and new suburbs have been seriously under-represented in this house. Nearly two years have passed since the last census, and it is clearly time for action. Since this task is to be undertaken by an independent commission, a considerable number of months must elapse before redistribution can be brought about, so I sincerely hope it will be possible to introduce the measure at an early date.
The statement of the administrator also indicates that the standing committee on privileges and elections is to examine the Canada Elections Act. It is interesting to note that both the Leader of the Opposition and the Prime Minister have agreed that campaigns should be shortened. I feel this is much to be desired. There is also agreement that some limitation on election expenses will have to be imposed. I think, also, that the recent legislation which has been introduced in the province of Quebec will have to be examined closely. In urban ridings the principle of dual enumeration has worked extremely well. I suggest we might consider extending this principle so as to have the deputy returning officer named by one party and the poll clerk by another. This would reduce the number of election day workers required. Provision should be made to allow many persons, including civil servants and their families as well as persons in hospitals, to mail their ballots if they are unavoidably absent on election day from their normal places of voting. I think, too, that free radio and television time should be used as far as possible to promote debates on an interparty basis between candidates in the ridings and the leaders of the national parties. Those of us who have had any familiarity with this medium are concerned about the effect of a trend toward placing it in the hands of public relations experts, who tend to produce a calculated image. A return to debates of a more spontaneous nature would, I think, be welcomed as being generally to the good.
The proposal to establish a municipal development and loan board will be welcomed, I am sure, by all municipalities across Canada. Those of us who have served on municipal councils know the tremendous demands on them for new works of all kinds, such as
88	HOUSE OF
The Address-Mr. Francis sewage disposal plants, sewers, water mains, roads, bridges, recreational facilities and a thousand other things. Measures such as federal loans to municipalities with forgiveness clauses for the development of sewage disposal facilities have set a pattern which has worked well. There is, I think, every reason to consider extending this pattern to other types of public loans. Careful administration, in co-operation with the provinces, of applications from rapidly growing communities whose credit has been strained to provide those municipal services now considered essential, will ensure success. New jobs will be created, and the burden of municipal property taxes lightened. Care should be taken not to disrupt local bond markets, or to make credit so easy that it would disrupt sound management of municipal budgets.
Closely associated with the program of the municipal development and loan board should be an expansion of federal assistance for urban renewal purposes. Older blighted areas should be redeveloped, but this requires capital on a scale not presently available to many municipalities.
The city of Ottawa, on whose council I have had the privilege of sitting for some years, should benefit from the new municipal development and loan board. The city of Ottawa has, however, a special and in many ways unique relationship to the federal government as part of the national capital region. As a municipality in its own right, the city of Ottawa is part of the national capital region. To members of the city council, members of parliament appear generally to be critical of city administration, especially of the potholes on Ottawa streets. The same members of parliament do not seem to be aware that the city borrows to the absolute maximum of its credit as permitted by the Ontario municipal board, and is seriously hampered by the inadequate grants in lieu of taxes paid by the largest employer in the area, namely the government of Canada. This chief employer makes demands for services, such as new bridges, which a private employer paying full taxes would have a right to expect. But the federal government does not pay what a private owner of property would pay to the city, and members of this house do not always seem aware of that fact.
Tonight I am offering my resignation to the council of the city of Ottawa in order to devote my full time to serving the city and the rest of the riding of Carleton as a member of this house. One of the matters which I hope the government will re-examine in the months ahead is the basis on which grants in lieu of taxes are paid by the federal government toward the development of the


national capital. The federal government develops its plans for the national capital through the national capital commission established by federal statute. As the administrator noted in his statement, these are times of great change, times that test old virtues. Great changes have occurred in this metropolitan area of the national capital region. The rate of growth in the years between the censuses of 1956 and 1961 was exceeded only by two metropolitan areas in Canada. It is time to re-examine the relations between the national capital commission and the elected municipal government, and indeed between municipal governments themselves. This task will involve close liaison with provincial and municipal representatives.
The members chosen by the federal government to sit on the national capital commission should be chosen on the basis of their ability to contribute to the development of a national capital. Narrow political loyalty should not be the basis of selection, nor should reward for party service, and I am confident that future appointments made by this government will be on the basis of ability to make contributions. The long term development of a national capital which will be a source of pride from one coast of Canada to the other suggests, I think, that appointees to the national capital commission should not engage in active campaigning on the hustings at election time, and should observe after appointment a rule of non-partisan behaviour in so far as this is possible.
Mr. Speaker, our party, through its most capable leader, the Prime Minister of Canada, is alive to the needs of our changing times. A program to restore faith in Canada, to relieve unemployment and to promote national development is being laid before this house. The task before us is a very great one indeed, a challenge as strong as that which any generation has ever faced. I am confident that this government and this parliament will be equal to it.

I could say a lot more, but it would cut into my time. I am loaded for bear, and I do not have the time to talk too much about Social Credit. I want to go into the question of chopping up the Department of Agriculture. In one fell swoop the marketing of grain was chopped off and put under the Department of Trade and Commerce again. That left production and certain other relatively small phases of marketing under the present Minister of Agriculture.
I go one step further. They have taken the remaining 50 per cent and chopped it in two. We are going to have an eastern minister of agriculture and a western minister of agriculture with equal status. In other words we are going to have a kind of east-west Grey cup game where there will be plenty of followers on each side, and I can assure you they will be rooting for their particular side. This action, instead of uniting Canada and bringing about a united country, is going to sow the seeds of dissension and division. It cannot result in anything else.
I have been asked a number of questions by farmers. One farmer asked me this question. He said, "If they are cutting the department down to one quarter, what is the reason? Have they cut it down to fit the size of the man available to fill it? If so will they cut the salary to one quarter?" So far as I know
[Mr. Kindt.)

there is only one country in the world that contemplates having two ministers of agriculture, which is what this government intends to do in Canada. This action is certain to promote nothing but confusion among the farmers and people generally. When our farmers want to know something about marketing, where are they going to go? If they want to know something about production, where are they going to go?
In other words, the department has been chopped up. If you look at the table of precedence as found on page 3 of the debates of the Senate for May 16, 1963 you will see that agriculture is 26th. It is right at the bottom of the totem pole. It is the caboose. In other words the government has ranked it as the least important of all departments in order of precedence. That is what this government thinks of the Department of Agriculture and the problems of agriculture.
We in western Canada all remember the three periods we have gone through. First of all there was the C. D. Howe period. The deputy minister to Mr. C. D. Howe is now the new Minister of Trade and Commerce. We all remember Mr. Howe's famous statement:
We have the best wheat in the world and if they want it let them come and get it.
There was no effort to get out and sell wheat. They simply took orders. Quotas were down to four bushels. Many farms in western Canada were abandoned. The cost-price squeeze forced them out of operation. As one who lived through that period I want to say that there was terrific distress among the farmers of western Canada. The bins were full of wheat, and all you have to do is talk to the farmers to know what took place during the C. D. Howe period. They depended upon the government for action but there was no action.
After the Progressive Conservative government came into power there was agitation to have the Department of Agriculture put back together again. That was done by putting the wheat board and also farm credit under the former minister of agriculture, one of the greatest leaders that agriculture has ever seen, Hon. Alvin Hamilton.
I do not need to tell you, Mr. Speaker, what has happened. I do not need to tell you about the sales of wheat to China and Japan, or how the wheat bins out west were emptied, or how the wheels started turning. All I have time to say is this. Under the direction of one man the farmers got results. There was co-ordination among the various branches of government. The minister of agriculture was able to tell the farmers, we want you to grow so much wheat, and if you grow it

we will market it for you. They loved it. They were told also how much barley to produce and how much oats to produce. This one man had his finger on the market and he also had his finger upon production. When you divide these two functions, what have you got? Nothing but chaos, nothing but false starts and stops, nothing but jealousy between departments and inaction.
As you know, since this government have come into power we have entered a third phase. They have torn the department apart again. They have put marketing back under trade and commerce and they have left production under the present minister. Everything is now arranged and they are back where they left off in 1957. The arrangement is perfect for them to go to sleep again. This is what the farmers of western Canada fear, and they might well be afraid of it.
If this government go back to sleep, if they lose these China sales, these 75 million bushels a year, then the quotas for western farmers may drop as low as five bushels per acre. These farmers are now enjoying almost unlimited quotas, say 10 bushels per acre, but they will find themselves in a position where they will have to go back to feeding pigs in order to get rid of their wheat. One of the first statements made by the new Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Sharp) was to the effect that he would not go behind the iron curtain to sell wheat. He made this clear the second day after he came into office. However, he had time to arrange a trip to Geneva. He put other things first. He also had in his mind, as the government had, that agriculture stood at the bottom of the list in terms of priorities. The minister's Geneva trip was far more important to him than putting forth every effort to retain wheat sales to China.
The government's efforts in so far as wheat sales are concerned are now divided. What the Department of Agriculture needs, what any organization needs if it is going to click, as any businessman can tell you, is one man in authority. One man must be able to wield the whip and get sales. This situation does not mean anything to the present government. They have divided the responsibility so they can all go back to sleep again.
Now I want to spend a minute or two on the question of industry. I notice that according to the speech from the throne a new department of industry is to be set up. According to the speech from the throne it is proposed to establish an area development agency. This agency will work with the provincial governments and other organizations to co-ordinate programs for parts of the country where, because of chronic unemployment, a special thrust for development is needed.
The Address-Mr. Kindt This government is going to use chronic unemployment areas as the touchstone or as the approach in deciding the location of new industry.
Then the speech from the throne indicates that we must create new industries. The fiscal and monetary policies of the government will give priority to the encouragement and expansion of industry. However, two approaches toward the question of the location of industry are revealed by what I see in the speech from the throne. One approach is the chronic unemployment area, and this is the approach this government intends to follow. The other approach, and the method which is usually followed under the free enterprise system, is to locate industries not in surplus unemployment areas but in those areas where they have the greatest economic advantage.
The surplus unemployment areas are mostly in Quebec and Ontario, as everyone knows. There are ten cabinet ministers from Ontario and eight from Quebec. These ministers have fixed up the speech from the throne, and I can see the handwriting of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) in it. Instead of deciding to locate industries in places in Canada where they would have the greatest chance of success, they have decided to put them in surplus labour areas. Instead of establishing industries in Alberta, the government intends to put them in Ontario and Quebec. If this criterion is followed the majority of the industries will be in Ontario and Quebec, with a few scattered over the other parts of the country.
If you investigate the free enterprise approach to the location of industries you will note that businessmen try to locate industries close to a supply of raw material. Where do these raw materials exist in the country? They exist in the prairie provinces and British Columbia. There is a great source of cheap hydrocarbons on the prairies. In fact there are tremendous quantities of hydrocarbons that are being flared because there are no industries available to use them. The country, and the people in the west, are crying aloud for new industry, but they are not going to get it under the new department of industry which is to be set up. The speech from the throne says:
It will be proposed that, within the new department, there will be established an area development agency. This agency will work with the provincial governments and other organizations to co-ordinate programs for parts of the country where, because of chronic unemployment, a special thrust for development is needed.
These industries are not going to be located in Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia because in most of those provinces there are not chronic unemployment areas

The Address-Mr. Moreau sufficient to justify the expenditure of public funds for new industries. The policy of putting these industries in the chronic unemployment areas is a trick or a method to be used by the government in order to locate industries in the east. Instead of having decentralization of industry and having industries spread all over western and eastern Canada, industries are to be located in Ontario and Quebec.

speechtext:
would like to offer my congratulations to you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, on your election to high office, and I also wish to compliment the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. Like them I am also a new member in the house, and I hope my maiden speech will approach the standards they have set for debate in this chamber.
The recent election campaign really began in my riding of York-Scarborough when the right hon. Prime Minister made his now historic stand on defence. The Scarborough speech, as it became known, was made at my nomination meeting on January 12, and it played a large part in precipitating the defeat of the last government. For this I believe most Canadians will be eternally grateful, and I would like to extend my thanks to the Prime Minister on his choice of location for that speech.
As most hon. members know, my riding is the most populous in Canada. For this reason I feel I bear a heavier responsibility than most in adequately representing, or attempting to represent, nearly 300,000 people. As a matter of fact quite a number of hon. members now sitting in the house are electors in my riding.
Although York-Scarborough is considered a dormitory by many, it is also a riding with many industries, farms and other varying interests. Its 163,000 electors represent a cross section of our country. Indeed most of them, like myself, are recent immigrants to the area, the largest number having migrated to the riding during the past 10 years. They come from every part of Canada and from many parts of the world, but while they have varying backgrounds and face many different problems they all share one common problem.

We in York-Scarborough live in a rapidly expanding suburban riding and face great difficulty in providing the new schools, hospitals and other municipal services so urgently needed. We know that municipal taxation cannot provide the necessary funds quickly enough. In particular, since 1956 the costs and difficulties of municipal borrowing have been crippling the development of our communities. Indeed, the foreign currency debt of Canadian municipalities is very unevenly distributed in Canada, and in fact three quarters of this debt presently outstanding has been incurred by seven urban centres in Canada, of which Toronto is one. The bulk of this foreign debt was incurred since 1956 and has added considerably to our currency exchange difficulties of recent years. I mention these facts to indicate that the creation of a municipal development and loan fund is long overdue, and it was with great pleasure that I heard the proposal to create such a fund in the speech from the throne.
I also heard with pleasure the announcement of a commission to undertake the redistribution of our electoral boundaries. This is a matter of prime concern to many hon. members from urban ridings, but it is of particular importance to the electors in my riding. Redistribution has been an election issue in York-Scarborough since 1957. Indeed my predecessor made it one of his prime election issues in all four campaigns since that time. Unfortunately he apparently was unable to get his government to give the matter very high priority, because nothing concrete was done. Meanwhile the riding keeps growing, and the problems of representing this large group of electors become more difficult, not to mention the difficulties of campaigning and the expenses involved in conducting an election campaign.
I could draw comparisons with ridings where constitutional guarantees exist, to which I am not opposed; but the inequities of representation even in the province of Ontario are considerable. The riding of Bruce, with a population of 30,000, has the same numerical representation in this house as my riding with a population of almost 300,000 people. At this rate, using 30,000 as the yardstick, my riding should have elected at least nine members, certainly sufficient to have corrected the minority situation which exists in the house. In this respect perhaps we can see a clue to the difficulties my predecessor encountered in achieving any results from his government on this matter.
I might add that the electors of my riding saw fit to give me the largest total vote recorded in Canadian history, really a result of the large size of the riding, and it is an

achievement I would not care to repeat. I am sure my wishes are shared by many hon. members when I say I hope the government will proceed with all speed to introduce legislation regarding the appointment of a commission to redraw our electoral boundaries. I was further heartened yesterday when, in debate, the Prime Minister reaffirmed the government's intention to proceed quickly in this matter.

National unity is a prerequisite to the solution of the other problems which we have to face at this time on the home front.
In my opinion, in the speech he made yesterday, the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) acknowledged that too small a number of English speaking Canadians understand those problems.
I should like to point out also that I am in favour of the adoption of a distinctive flag. In the course of my work and of my travels in practically every corner of this country, I noticed that most Canadians share my views in this connection.

There is also, Mr. Speaker, the matter of regulations governing the development of resources on Indian reservations. We should not become so immersed in the problems of government as to forget what made yesterday. Our party, sitting in opposition, which in itself is an institution in accordance with British parliamentary practice, is favoured by the fact that its great leader has been re-elected. There is no doubt that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefen-baker), even though as prime minister he encountered the most difficult years in the history of our country, performed an excellent job. Mr. Speaker, the head of the present government (Mr. Pearson), made a poor showing during the last electoral campaign. He contradicted himself from beginning to end on the question of nuclear arms. speechtext:
That is what newspapers like he Devoir and La Presse reported. I would not want the member for Hull to insult newspapermen. I know he has a great deal of consideration for them.
Mr. Speaker, I should now like to list the reasons of our defeat.
(1)	There was an inflow of U.S. dollars to ensure that Canada would become an American satellite.
(2)	Numerous promises were made.
(3)	Support was given by Quebec.
After the election, American finance was used to try to buy off several members of parliament.
In Le Devoir of May 14, 1963, the hon. member for Sherbrooke (Mr. Chapdelaine) is reported as saying during a caucus in Ottawa, that $50,000 in American funds were offered to him as the price of his open support of the Liberal party. And what about the six Social Credit members?
The premier of Newfoundland (Mr. Smallwood) and the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate (Mr. Pickersgill) who spent some time in Nassau after the election, could shed some light on this matter.
I would recommend that the government convene immediately the committee on privileges and elections to clear up this smelly business and to punish those who have tried to bribe members of the parliament of Canada.
A great deal of publicity was given to the number of Quebec members who were appointed to the cabinet.
Quantity does not mean quality.
I have here an excerpt from the newspaper Le Devoir of April 23, 1963, which I quote:
Has Mr. Pearson chosen the most dynamic elements of his Quebec deputation? One feels that there was a compromise. On the one hand, the old guard: Messrs. Lionel Chevrier (whose selection was a must), Azellus Denis and Jean-Paul Descha-telets (the least that can be said about them being that their selection was not a must), as well as Mr. Lucien Cardin, who replaces Mr. Sevigny.
On the other hand, the newcomers: Mr. Maurice Lamontagne to a position of honour-probably temporary-but not of influence; Mr. Guy Favreau to immigration, and Mr. Rene Tremblay, without portfolio.
Those whose absence is disappointing but can be easily explained: Messrs. Maurice Sauve and Jean-Luc Pepin-the former because he had become the symbol of the new frontier and was sacrificed to the backbenchers, the latter because he has just arrived.
In short, the "young'' team is relegated to the bottom of the ladder. Make way for the good old Liberal stalwarts.
For the moment, therefore, we are gaining in number but very little in quality and in influence.
And I am quoting from the April 27, 1963 issue of the newspaper La Presse:
But what about his actions?

That is the question. If we were right now to judge Mr. Pearson on the appointments he has just made to the ministry, we would have to infer that he has not understood a great deal about the aspirations of the French Canadian people in 1963. He has behaved like a sort of immature Mackenzie King, who has made some progress in arithmetic but very little in sociology-
And the article goes on to say:
Who has been appointed at the head of the departments of Finance, of Defence, of Trade and Commerce, of Industry, and of Defence Production? Messrs. Gordon, Hellyer, Sharp and Drury.

Maurice Lamontagne, Rene Tremblay and Maurice Sauve. During the last campaign, Mr. Lesage had Mr. Pearson elected in Ottawa so that Quebec 28902-5-74

It will be remembered that just before the election, the premier of Quebec requested from Ottawa a revision of the tax structure (in particular 25 per cent of the personal income tax) as a condition for his support of Mr. Pearson.

The speech from the throne is for neofederalism. There is no mention of a decentralization of the powers of taxation. The right hon. Prime Minister is not even aware of Mr. Lesage's ultimatum. The speech of the throne, in my opinion, is essentially a document of centralization.

Therefore, it seems that the subsidies paid by the central government to the provinces are inevitable at the present time and are firmly established in our political tradition. Mr. Lesage and the present leader of the federal government were those mainly responsible for centralization a few years ago, on the advice of the hon. member for Outre-mont-St. Jean. Today, Mr. Lesage is backing out and is becoming an autonomist. I am not blaming him, but I shall question his sincerity towards the province of Quebec as long as he does nothing to force Ottawa to beat a retreat as a Quebec premier did before. Mr. Lesage has not even delivered his ultimatum in writing to Ottawa. Is he being sincere, Mr. Speaker?
The premier of Quebec showed weakness in his demands, that is in asking for the return of 25 per cent of the personal and corporation income tax and 100 per cent of the succession duties.
He should insist upon 100 per cent of the personal and corporation income tax. And should Ottawa refuse to give in, let Mr. Lesage take steps. Then we shall know how sincere he is.
In addition, Mr. Lesage should demand:
1.	That the federal government withdraw from joint programs;
2.	That censure at the C.B.C. come under the government of the province of Quebec;
3.	That the federal government withdraw from the field of education;
4.	That Indian affairs and those of the Eskimos of new Quebec come solely under the administration of the province of Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, confederation is now in danger.
Here are, for instance, the amounts collected in Quebec by the federal government in 1961-62 as direct taxes only.
Personal income tax $469,827,176 Corporation income tax 405,352,708 Non-resident income tax 35,540,690 Estate tax	14,991,904
Total	$925,722,478
By comparison, let us note that during the same period the total revenue of the Quebec government from direct and indirect taxes was only $754,107,000. So, the amount paid each year to Ottawa in taxes is larger than the total revenue of the Quebec government.
At present, Mr. Speaker, the province of Quebec collects 17 per cent of the personal income tax and less than 11 per cent of the corporation income tax. As far as the estate tax is concerned, Quebec collects about 50 per cent.
Not only the province of Quebec, but every province in the confederation is sinking into debts.
For instance, the province of Quebec, these last few years, has imposed 12 new taxes to meet its needs. First of all, the Quebec taxpayers are bearing a total debt of about $6 billion, if we add up the liabilities of the province, of the municipalities and of the school boards. Second, the direct and indirect debt of the Quebec government will then amount to $3,700 million, that is close to $4 billion. The average per capita debt in Quebec amounts to $675.
For the 1963-64 fiscal year, the Quebec government forecasts a $146 million deficit.
Here is the progression of the deficits:

For instance, Mr. Speaker, the Montreal Catholic school board cost the taxpayers some $54 million in 1961-62.

the province of Quebec, adds up to the colossal amount of $500 million.
Needless to add, Mr. Speaker, that the provincial farm credit fund is empty. Sometimes, the highway department employees do not get their pay. Several classical colleges in the province of Quebec are seeking university charters; such is the case of the Loyola College, the Seminaire de Trois-Rivieres and the College Sainte-Marie.
Everybody is hard pressed in the province of Quebec, for the provincial government has a responsibility and a mandate to fulfil as regards the cultural and educational requirements of the province. But the federal government had centralized all taxation powers. And that is due to ingenuity of the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean.
Mr. Speaker, under the Conservative government, we had started this decentralization. During the fiscal year ended March 31, 1963, Quebec received subsidies in the amount of some $517 million while in 1957, under a government of which Mr. Lesage himself was a member, Quebec received only $177 million.
Our government raised from 10 to 20 per cent the deductible portion of the federal income tax for provincial purposes. Today, the province of Quebec collects up to 16 per cent. We wanted to keep on with that decentralization, but with the help of the Social Crediters, Mr. Speaker, the Liberals defeated us and prevented us from going ahead and giving back to the provinces more taxation powers. Mr. Speaker, the Quebec government wants to develop and to take care of the economical, educational and cultural needs of the province. Quebec wants to become a giant within confederation, to save Canada from American annexation.
I am not in favour for a moment of convening of the states-general to review the Canadian constitution.
Ottawa should start proving its good faith and retire from the taxation field which is, in fact, the responsibility of the provinces. Then we could convene the states-general to adapt the constitution to our contemporary life and extend the French fact from coast to coast. Let us first of all come back to the basic principles of Sir John Macdonald and Sir Georges Etienne Cartier. Otherwise, Quebec will separate itself from confederation and we shall, in 1967, witness the disintegration of the Canadian confederation.
The Address-Mr. Caouette
I shall conclude, Mr. Speaker, by quoting from an article published in the local papers of Joliette city and its region, by the "Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste du Diocese de Joliette Inc." I take pleasure in reading out that article published on February 27, 1963 and entitled:
Confederation-The various currents of opinion which are now noticed in Quebec show an evident and generalized discontent among the population. The various positions expressed show the need of reforming the system established in 1867.
We believe that those responsible for Canadian policy will definitely have to undertake an early study of our present constitution in order to give it a new direction.
It is obvious that the present state of affairs does not satisfy anybody now. The statements of French Canadian political leaders and the sprouting of numerous independence movements among our population are an indisputable sign of discontent at this time.
We therefore invite the people to make use of its influence to convince the political leaders of the need for undertaking a complete study of the present problems and to bring about some solution which, while observing the fundamental rights of the various communities, will satisfy their respective aspirations and allow them to develop in harmony and good will.
It is signed:
"La Societe Saint-Jean-Baptiste du Diocese de Joliette Inc.; Rene Charette, chief secretary."
Mr. Speaker, in concluding, I hope the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean will write another book, and this time give a fair deal to the provinces so as to redress the bad service he rendered confederation. And I say, Mr. Speaker, that, following the advice they got from the hon. member for Outremont-St. Jean, those who sit on the other side of the house are responsible for the conflict and the turmoil of ideas which now exist in Canada, and more particularly in French speaking Canada. That is why I urge this government to reverse steam and go on with the decentralization in order to save Canadian confederation.

Mr. Speaker, those are replies to the questions which several candidates asked the people during the electoral campaign. They were reported on television, for instance, and on the radio-as did the member for St. Jean-Iberville-Napierville (Mr. Dupuis)-thus leading the public to believe that the Social Credit party would print money inconsiderately and without restraint and that we would flood Canada with currency as was the case in Germany in 1923 and 1924.

Thus, the problems which face us at this time and which are mentioned in the speech from the throne-to which I will come back in a few minutes-those situations and problems to which there are no solutions, as I say, are due to a financial system which has grown fatter on its deathbed than when it was born.
Mr. Speaker, all kinds of things were made up in the province of Quebec. My Liberal friends in that province bought full pages in La Presse, Le Devoir and other large newspapers in the province of Quebec to insinuate, for example, that Social Credit would create misery and inflation in Canada, whereas inflation is the result of an administration such as the present one.
When a municipal council borrows $300,000 or $3,000,000 to build a city hall, at a yearly interest rate of 5 per cent for a period of 20 years, the taxpayers have to pay back $600,000 for a $300,000 loan and $6 million for a $3 million loan. The $300,000 city hall will never be worth $600,000; on the contrary, it will be worth less and less as the years go by. But the people will still have to pay $600,000. That is true inflation. That is the kind of administration that the Conservatives and the Liberals have given us in turn.
The Address-Mr. Caouette
Mr. Speaker, I will now deal with the speech from the throne, which talks glibly about biculturalism, the co-existence of the two great nations in Canada, the French and the Anglo-Saxon nations.
On the day parliament opened, together with our colleagues from all corners of the house we attended the splendid reception offered to the representative of Her Majesty.
The guard of honour and what was presumably its own brass band, faced the parliament buildings. His Excellency the Governor General-who, 1 trust, will very-soon recover-was represented by an Administrator, the Chief Justice of the Supreme Court. We witnessed an impressive state pageant, truly beautiful and imposing. We welcomed Her Majesty's representative with the hymn "God Save the Queen", and I think this was as it should have been.
However, I wonder why we did not also hear the strains of "O, Canada"?
If, as we are told, it is essential that our two cultures should co-exist in Canada, we from Quebec have absolutely no objection to the "God Save the Queen"; but we feel that on such an occasion we should also have heard "O Canada", so dear to the heart of all Canadians, our national anthem.
Mr. Speaker, we also did note the absence -and I can just see the hon. member for Mercier (Mr. Boulanger), who is always somewhat nervous in similar circumstances -and this was so much the case when he heard "O Canada" being sung that he could not but smile.
Why did we not have a distinctive national flag at that time? I remember that in 1956-57, when the Conservatives had taken over, we expected to have a distinctive national flag. I hope that during all those years in the opposition the Liberals had the opportunity of studying the feasibility of giving Canada a distinctive national flag and a national anthem.
During the month of February, I had the privilege, right at the start of the election campaign, of visiting a country which is part of the British commonwealth of nations. I went to Jamaica. Now the first gesture of the Jamaican government when that country became independent in August 1962, was to adopt an authentic national anthem for Jamaica, as well as a distinctive national Jamaican flag. So the first gesture of a small country, practically trailing behind all other commonwealth countries, was to adopt its

The Address-Mr. Caouette own flag and anthem, without a single emblem, either English, or French, or Spanish, without any outward sign of assimilation.
Now, we are asking for the same thing in Canada. We do not want a flag with a French emblem. As far as France is concerned, we have great respect for that country, in the same way as we respect England. But, we are first and foremost, Canadians. We want, in the first instance, Canadians to understand each other. We are not separatists. We want a Canada where people may understand one another, where Canadians would be able to speak to each other-a thing which is but rarely found here, in spite of all the election shenanigans we witnessed on April 8 last.
Mr. Speaker, another point to which I want to call the attention of all hon. members, whether they be French or English speaking, is that when we use the parliamentary telephone for a long distance call, nine times out of ten, we are told: "I'm sorry, I do not speak French. Would you like a French operator?" That happens nine times out of ten. I do not care in the least whether the operator's name is Bradshaw, MacDonald, Choquette or Dupuis as long as she is able to talk to me in my own language.
I think we should start by bringing about a respect of our country's dual culture within the parliamentary framework-not because we bear a grudge against those who do not know French, but because we want to be up to date in our demands with regard to the respect due to the two elements of Canada, which should be placed on an equal footing.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne mentioned many fine things, serious and elaborate, which we mentioned many times ourselves in this house. I see, for instance, the following words in the speech from the throne, and I quote:
These are times that test old virtues. They are times that open up new opportunities. Familiar ways of thought and action are becoming less certain guides.
The familiar ways of thought are personified by the economists of the Liberal party.
The familiar ways of thought and action are becoming less certain guides.
We are not certain anymore.
Many old paths are no longer open to us. The task before us is to seek out with wisdom and imagination-
Where will they take that imagination, since they have had none for the past 50 or 75 years? Is it with the kind of imagination they displayed in the province of Quebec dur-

ing the last election that they will make us believe they are serious and sincere, when they say that those new paths will lead us surely forward?
What are those new paths? Is it the moon, the planet Mars or some space system? I do not know. Nothing definite, nothing factual.
They talk about new paths while we have been saying ourselves in the province of Quebec for the last 20 years, and also across Canada, that the present old finance system can only lead to complete and total failure. That failure, the previous government did not want to face it and if this government faces it without taking drastic measures to bring the finance system to reason in Canada, it will soon be the end of the road for our staggering democracy. And as long as they keep going over the same path, it will be a huge and total failure. And later on, it is said:
But they depend on our overcoming serious problems. It is only with courage and perseverance and hard work that we will achieve the better life that is within our power, for ourselves and for our children.
Which Canadians are lacking courage and perseverance? Which Canadians have refused to work for the development and progress of our national inheritance? I think I have a right to say that those who lacked courage are the representatives of the people in the federal government, and also the representatives of the people in the federal parliament have lacked perseverance. And I think that the governments which succeeded each other since confederation have failed to work with zeal.
Our progress is the work of all the people.
At last, here is a true fact.
The determination of my ministers is that the government through its policies will contribute the leadership, the purpose, the decision that are its responsibilities to the people.
The people have been waiting for a long time and are more and more anxious. For a long time, the electors have been looked after only at election time and in order to juggle the popular vote, all that is done is to try and make them believe that the government in power is the one which received a mandate from the nation, when in fact, the votes of the people are obtained through fear, under threat, under the threat of losing their jobs or their pensions, and it happened in Canada on April 8 last. This is a sharp contrast with the fine wording of the speech from the throne.

Mr. Speaker, a great many matters are mentioned in the speech from the throne, but no details are given. When the government states for instance, that:
It will foster the spirit of co-operative federalism, fully respecting the rights of the provinces while safeguarding and extending the equality of opportunity which properly belongs to all Canadians in all parts of our country. In these purposes, as in others, my ministers will seek frequent consultation with the governments of the provinces.
We are in favour of respecting the rights of the provinces, but let not the federal government assume alone the right to determine the needs of the provinces without consulting them. While listening earlier to the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Mont-calm (Mr. Pigeon), I was thinking that they should have initiated those consultations themselves since they were in power from 1957.
In particular, my ministers will strive to lessen international tensions and halt the arms race by seeking measures of controlled disarmament, including a treaty to end nuclear tests under reasonable safeguards.
For this purpose, the armed forces of Canada should have available the modern weapons necessary to perform effectively the defensive tasks which Canada has undertaken in the alliance.
Mr. Speaker, that is a bit steep.

Mr. Speaker, the amendment moved by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) deals with nuclear weapons. We in the province of Quebec, together with other Canadians across the country, have taken a stand in that regard. We have stated our opposition to armaments and war, and I will tell you why.
We do not believe in the possibility of nuclear war any more than we believe in the possible use of bacteriological gases such as those which were used in the years 1914-18. As soon as the Russians, the British and the Germans realized that the winds could turn and push the gases back to their senders they met and decided: "Let us not use gas warfare, it is too dangerous. We can throw gases which may come back in our own face and then we may turn out to be the loser." The same situation would develop as far as nuclear warfare is concerned.
But nuclear weapon manufacturers are interested in producing such weapons. In my opinion, instead of following the path of destruction, the Canadian government should
The Address-Mr. Caouette play the part of a peacemaker and invite all the nations of the world, including Russia, to promote peace and to guarantee the security and freedom of men, putting nuclear power at the service of men, instead of preparing it for the annihilation of humanity. That simply is the position we have adopted in defining our aims and our ideal in Canada and in Quebec.
Mr. Speaker, when I had the privilege of visiting Jamaica, a small and poor country where there is extreme poverty, I noticed that people in that country were not asking at all for nuclear weapons or atomic bombs but quite contrary they needed money that we now appropriate for atomic warfare. That money would help them to buy bread, butter, clothes and houses because they too are entitled to live as men, as creatures of God. And if our country undertook to do that it would give an example of true peace and of unity in the brotherhood of nations and that can become a reality provided we act in good faith.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne also deals with industrial expansion. Now, I come from an industrial area, the mining area of Quebec where there are gold, copper and zinc mines. There are also to be found vast forests and large farms. But the economy of the area, and more particularly that of the counties of Villeneuve, Chapleau and part of Temiscamingue, is based on mining.
Our area has a great number of mining prospects and it would only be delighted to increase their development. The prospectors could make more discoveries, and the industrialists could set up more mills; should the government decide immediately to raise by $10 an ounce the price for Canadian gold, we would see a great number of new mining companies spring up in our area. Thousands of people would thus find profitable employment, while thousands of others would continue to manufacture other products in that area, which has been practically undeveloped so far.
I would also suggest that the government grant a yearly increase of 3 per cent to new production of gold. Such a step would revive the economical life of our area, especially in the riding of Villeneuve, and nobody would suffer from it. Moreover, the setting up of these new mining companies in our area would bring additional revenue to the government and would help to create more jobs for the people who are now loafing in certain towns, in the northwestern part of the province of Quebec, and throughout the province.

The Address-Mr. Caouette It is beyond doubt that such a policy would bring about employment opportunities, and we would thus contribute to the revival of the economic life of our area and, indirectly, to the improvement of the whole Canadian economy.
The same suggestion could apply to the Elliot Lake district where hundreds of houses, now empty, had to be taken over by Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. The people who bought those houses five, six or seven years ago have lost all their life's savings. Citizens are idle in an area where it would be possible to set up new industries or promote the re-opening of mines which are already shut down, by signing agreements or contracts with the United States, England or other countries where uranium could be used, just like copper and zinc are being used today to bring about new production opportunities in our country.
Mr. Speaker, the speech from the throne does not contain any definite statement on the setting up of a department of industry. What will be the functions of such a department? What will it promote? Will it set up an organization to which industry can look for advice? Industry is ready to do everything it can to increase production.
As the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson), our leader, mentioned last night, Mr. G. L. Barber, an economist, and professor at the University of Manitoba, spoke to the point when he said that the injection of $1 billion into the Canadian economy would contribute to its recovery and to its continuous development. That theory is not very remote from the policy the Social Crediters have long advocated.
Instead of considering national production on a productive basis or with regard to the potential production, we should consider the whole of the economy of Canada from the point of view of the consumer, for it is the consumer who, after all, will get the whole Canadian industry moving. The consumer who will have sufficient purchasing power to buy the products manufactured for him shall order from industry; industry will be operating and thousands of unemployed will become employees who will contribute to the development of our common inheritance and who will help to establish peace, justice, security and abundance for each and everyone of us.

Mr. Speaker, this may sound repetitious, but I should like to add my congratulations to yourself upon your unanimous appointment as chairman of committees of the whole and Deputy Speaker of this House of Commons. I am certain you will find the experience most interesting and exhilarating. Through you, sir, may I convey my congratulations to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. Mac-naughton) on his appointment to Speaker of this house. I convey these congratulations with a great deal of sincerity because of my association with our present Speaker during the time he was chairman of our public accounts committee. It must have been a most unique experience for the hon. member to be the first opposition member in the history of this house, as far as my knowledge goes, to be appointed chairman of such an important committee. I can say, sir, without any hesitation whatsoever that I think it was the leadership he gave us and the impartiality he showed which made the public accounts committee over the years one of the most interesting, influential and powerful committees ever known in the history of this House of Commons. I know that the impartiality, understanding and compassion he showed in that committee will be carried forward into his honoured position as our Speaker.
Although this may sound a little impertinent or impudent, Mr. Speaker, may I say, in concluding these remarks and anticipating that he will do such a remarkable job that in so doing he will have to find, as experience in this house has already shown, firmness together with impartiality and compassion, otherwise a few individuals may try to take advantage of his compassion and reasonableness.
This leads me to the next subject about which I should like to make a few remarks. I sincerely hope that all the words which have been spoken in this debate will be followed through with action in the appointment of a committee of this House of Commons to make an early study and, I hope, early decision on the standing orders and procedures of this house. Sir, I have had a little experience in parliament, always in opposition, although there is always the hope of a change. Because of that experience I must say that we are 265 directors of the biggest business of this country. Therefore it is without doubt somewhat difficult to work out standing orders and procedures which can cover everything. However, I have no hesitation in saying, even if I may be called an independent thinker and something of a renegade, that we can do a lot more than we have ever done in the past

toward expediting the business of the people by some reforms in our procedures and standing orders.
I hope, although this might be considered to be almost rebellious, that in the considerations of this committee-which I hope will be appointed very soon-they will give real study to the problems of expediting the business of the people as well as the necessity of all members having full rights of expression. I hope, sir-and may I say that I am speaking personally; I have not taken it up with the other members of our group-that some way will be found to stop some of the useless repetition that holds us up for days unnecessarily in the house. I hope some method will be found of outlining in detail just what is a question of urgency under the orders of the day. I hope some method will be found whereby those things that belong on the order paper will be put on the order paper, and some method of deciding just how many supplementary questions should be asked on one question under orders of the day.
I also hope, sir, that something will be done toward giving consideration to the appointment of select standing committees of this house. To me, quite bluntly, it has always been, I would say, stupid and asinine to have under our standing orders, as we have under standing order 65, committees of this house composed of 50 or 60 members of whom 10, 15 or 20 shall constitute a quorum. It is my firm conviction that serious consideration should be given to some revamping of standing order 65 in order that we may have not only committees which work efficiently but committees with as close to full attendance as possible, and not attendance just once in a while when decisions are made-which has happened in the past- when it comes to a vote, by members who were never in the committee when the data, information and facts were before the committee. These, sir, are some of the things which I believe should be considered. If considered properly and efficiently and decided upon by the members of this house in a responsible way, we can do much to expedite the business of the house and see that we achieve a great deal more efficiency than has been possible in the past.

Well, I do not think I have been absent from this chamber for many minutes since the session opened, and we have seen members of Her Majesty's most loyal official opposition rising in their places and 28902-5-84
