Mr. Speaker, perhaps at this time the 265 members who make up this House of Commons have greater responsibility than ever before, because for approximately 18 months the business of Canada was brought to a halt. For almost 18 months there was too much rehashing of the previous election and campaigning for the next. There are too many problems which have to be faced- too many decisions which have to be made. It is, therefore, my sincere hope, and I know it is the hope of this group in the House of Commons, that we shall face our responsibility in a proper manner as Canadians elected to do a job first and to be political partisans second. I have already said that I feel a good deal of time has been lost in previous parliaments because of unnecessary and useless repetition. I do not want to be

The Address-Mr. Winch guilty of that myself. Therefore, I do not intend to comment at any length on what is contained in the speech from the throne. The most important aspects of the attitude taken by this group have already been outlined by our leader, the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas). All I wish to say is that I find myself in agreement with his general statement that there are a number of proposals in the speech from the throne which could undoubtedly prove of benefit in the long run to the Canadian economy and to the Canadian people provided the legislation itself, when it is brought down, embodies the principles contained in the government's program. We shall therefore have to wait until the legislation is introduced before we are in a position to make specific and detailed comment.
However, much as I agree with long range planning-and such planning has been required for many, many years-I do want to say I was bitterly disappointed that there was not some indication that the government intends to put into effect the immediate measures which are required to handle some of the problems facing Canada. It is all very fine for the Liberals to campaign for one million jobs in five years. It is very fine to have something in the speech from the throne about long range planning through the establishment of councils or boards which will have an impact in years to come, as I hope it will. But, Mr. Speaker, that does not clothe and shelter the half million persons presently unemployed.
I should like to say-and I say this with full knowledge of what I am saying-that I had the privilege of spending 20 years in the parliament of British Columbia and I have now spent 10 years in this House of Commons. But never as in the two months preceding the opening of this house did I have as many visitors or phone calls to my home from people unemployed saying: "For God's sake, Winch, can you get me a job?" Nor did I have so many who were going off unemployment insurance because their payments had run out, or who were already off it. And what could I as an individual member of this house give to those heads of families in need of immediate attention? The Liberals said that they had the answer, and they did not say during the campaign that the answer would be forthcoming three or five years from now. They said they would have the answer when they took office. Mr. Speaker, there is not a thing in the speech from the throne to indicate any action to take care of the immediate problem of the half million unemployed and of those who are in a different category.

That brings me to something else. I do not know what was said by the Liberals across Canada during the campaign, but I do know that in B.C. in general, and in Vancouver in particular, they were interested in the training of our youth, in higher education for our youth. They were interested in seeing that our youth had the opportunity, irrespective of their family income, of getting that education. Yet I can assure you, sir, that each day before I came back to this house I had boys and girls coming to my home who were going into their last year at university, whose parents were not able to pay for that last year and to maintain them. They were themselves unable to obtain employment. Are they to be denied? While the Liberal party said they had the immediate answer in British Columbia, and the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) said they had the immediate answer in Vancouver, that there would be 10,000 scholarships and the opportunity to take care of these people, the payment of their fees and their maintenance, I find no word of this in the speech from the throne. We have had no indication yet from anyone on the government side of the house as to what is going to be done for those young people in their last year or their second last year at university.
Surely, sir, it is not carping criticism, it is not irresponsibility, for us to draw this to the attention of the government and to ask them when they are going to act and how soon. Because the need is now, not three, four or five years from now. We agree with long range planning, but we do not want people to starve to death and not be able to take advantage of it in, we hope, the not too distant future. In the few days which lie ahead during this debate we hope that we will hear something from the government about the immediate emergency plans for those in need now, both with regard to the unemployed and with regard to education.
Now, Mr. Speaker, in the balance of time at my disposal I want to comment on the subamendment moved by our leader. May I remind you of the wording:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have indicated their intention of acquiring nuclear arms for Canadian forces, thereby lessening the chances for nuclear disarmament and increasing the danger of nuclear war.
Mr. Speaker, this is a matter not only of major concern to every member of the New Democratic party, but also to the people of Canada, and indirectly through this Canadian House of Commons to the people of the world. I had the honour of being a Canadian delegate-observer at the United Nations in 1960. I have followed the speeches at the

United Nations by Canadian delegates since 1960. I was a very proud man to hear the representations made in the United Nations by Canadian official spokesmen. I heard them in plenary session and in the No. 1 political committee speaking on subjects such as the cessation of nuclear testing, no expansion of the nuclear club, and general and complete disarmament along the lines laid down by Mr. Wadsworth when he was the United States ambassador, and which, it was suggested, could be accomplished in five or six years. Being so proud of the Canadian stand I would go into the lounge or into the corridors and hear the Afro-Asian delegates say: "You in Canada speak with a forked tongue. You talk this way at the United Nations, you act this way in the disarmament committee in Geneva, but at home you purchase weapons which can only be utilized if they have a nuclear warhead". Mr. Speaker, that was a keen disappointment to me and I maintain a double cross of the people of Canada, because you cannot speak one way outside of Canada and act another way inside Canada. Nor can I see any difference between the preceding government and the present one as regards talking with a forked tongue.
Moreover, Mr. Speaker, I cannot accept the statements we have received thus far that decisions have to be made because of previous commitments. I find that what I heard when I attended as a delegate to NATO in 1961 and what I heard from NORAD in no way coincides with the position taken by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). If I may briefly refer to that, with regard to NORAD it was my understanding from reading the newspapers that the Minister of National Defence said we were going to have nuclear warheads for our Bomarcs in Canada because this was a commitment made by the previous government. If the present government says that it is a commitment, then I cannot understand why on January 9 General John K. Gerhart, commander of the north American air defence system, said that there was no commitment to NORAD that Canada assume nuclear weapons or nuclear warheads.
This morning I had the opportunity of doing a double check to make sure that I had this correct. The Ottawa Journal of January 9 reports General Gerhart as having said:
Lack of nuclear arms in Canada has not altered NORAD'S over-all planning. General Gerhart made his comment while here to inspect the Bomarc and semi-automatic ground environment defence complex which form part of the NORAD set-up. The U.S. army officer stated Canada was not committed to nuclear arms under NORAD and this position was well known when NORAD was formed.
Surely General Gerhart, commander of the North American air defence system, knows
The Address-Mr. Winch what he is talking about. I presume he does. He also said, and this is in quotation marks:
"Whether we have them here in North Bay or not is not germane to our planning."
On that basis I fail to understand why our Prime Minister, a Nobel peace prize winner, says that under NORAD we are committed to equipping our weapons with nuclear warheads. Moreover, the Bomarc is a defence against the manned bomber. Will he please explain this? I have here the Vancouver Province of January 31 last containing a Washington news service dispatch in which United States defence secretary McNamara makes it very clear that the problem in a future war is not the manned bomber, but the missile. I am not going to quote the article but it is here. I draw the attention of hon. members to the fact that McNamara said this on January 31 last.
Did hon. members read the Globe and Mail this morning? What does secretary of defence McNamara say in appearing before a congressional committee?
The great problem is that in a missile age we must assume the Soviets will first attack with missiles before their bombers attack and almost certainly among the targets for their missile attack would be our SAGE centres, in which case they would be out of operation before the bombers arrive.
Warning against an intercontinental missile attack comes through huge, powerful radar fences constructed in the far north, in Alaska and Greenland. No accurate western way of shooting down these intercontinental ballistic missiles exists yet.
Here we have Mr. McNamara, as reported in this morning's Globe and Mail, saying that any attack will be a missile attack first. The missile attack will be on our SAGE installations of which Canada only has one, that at North Bay where we have the Bomarc, and that installation will be blown up before the manned bomber comes against which the Bomarc installation is supposed to defend us.
We simply ask in all reasonableness that the House of Commons be taken a little more into the confidence of the government on this matter and that we be given a little more information.
What I have said about NORAD also applies to NATO. I am sorry I only have another four minutes. It is difficult to say in four minutes what I want to say about NATO but I am going to try. NATO was formed as a military alliance, perhaps a necessary and essential one at that time. I had the privilege of being one of the House of Commons delegates to the NATO parliamentary association meeting in Paris in November of 1961. The other delegates must confirm what I am about to say and if they do not they had better watch out because on my desk I have a transcript of every word said there.

The Address-Mr. Pearson
Information was given us in 1961, not only by General Norstad, then the commander of NATO, but by leading speakers from other countries in NATO, that perhaps too much emphasis had been placed on the nuclear deterrent and that the great need was the building up of conventional forces. It was said at that conference that the country that could perhaps best build up the necessary, mobile, trained, conventional force was Canada. That is on the record.
Much has been said in recent weeks by NATO members and in the United States by the president himself about the need for the building up of a conventional force because any move in Europe outside of an all-out war will be a probing attack, and such an attack will be by conventional weapons. In 1961 at the NATO conference it was said that such an attack must be repelled by conventional weapons because if we use tactical nuclear weapons that will bring about a strategic nuclear war. This is all a matter of record. Why do we not follow it up?

Mr. Speaker, I regret that I have to intervene again in this debate but the subamendment moved by the hon. member for Burn-aby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) and the terms in which he moved it, with some challenging references to myself, make it necessary for me to place before the house the position of the government in respect of the subamendment, which is very clear indeed in its terms, Mr. Speaker, though not, as I hope to point out, quite so clear in its implications.
I regret that the hon. member who has just sat down was not able to complete his remarks because they are always interesting and always listened to with attention by members of the house. He emphasized that he will perhaps forgive me for calling the righteous consistency of his party in these and other matters. It is interesting to recall, though I did not have very much opportunity to do as much research as I would have liked in recalling it, the position of the New Democratic party and its predecessor, the C.C.F. party, in respect of this matter of nuclear defence.
As I ventured to say earlier in this debate, NATO accepted a nuclear commitment for the alliance as far back as December 19, 1957, when at the council meeting of that year the communique stated, and I repeat, that NATO, not any individual member but NATO, "has decided to establish stocks of nuclear warheads which will be readily available for the

defence of the alliance in case of need". Was there a violent or any other kind of reaction in this house from the C.C.F. party of that day to that communique, to that result of the NATO council meeting of that time which was reported in this house four days later by the prime minister of that day on December 21, 1957, in terms set out at page 2721 of Hansard"! This is one paragraph only from his statement:
We had to ensure that the NATO defence structure, first erected to meet the needs of 1949, was adjusted to meet the needs of 1957, to render impregnable, as I said a moment ago, the defensive capacity of the Atlantic community in the nuclear era.
That statement was made by the prime minister of that time after a decision taken by the government of that day to agree to NATO taking on a nuclear commitment for the coalition; and I would have thought, if my hon. friends were as consistent as they boast about being, that they would have reacted to that first commitment by Canada to NATO nuclear defence as they have reacted recently to statements from this side of the house. But, Mr. Speaker, there was no such reaction. There was no reference in the debate from which I have just quoted to the fact the government of the day was irresponsible or contemptuous of parliament in not consulting and getting the approval of parliament before it made this commitment. The government of that day had the right to take on that commitment as a member of a coalition, come back to parliament as it did and make the announcement of what it had done. It was the right of parliament, then, to accept or repudiate that commitment. This is responsible government, as I ventured to point out last night when quoting the prime minister of that day in support of my contention.
There was no complaint about the procedure that was followed at that time. In fact, the comment by the leader of the C.C.F. party at that time on the substance of the decision made was very, very mild indeed, although that began the process of making NATO into a nuclear defensive power to meet the new kind of threat which faced the members of NATO at that time. So it went on for a couple of years. There was very little reference in this house by any member of the C.C.F. to the inequity of this decision or subsequent decisions that the government of that day took on the roles which could only be fulfilled effectively by the use of nuclear ammunition for weapon systems which had been acquired.
I am not going to quote remarks made in the intervening years. However, it was not until 1960 that I was able to find any change in the opinion of the members of the C.C.F.

party, the predecessor of the New Democratic party. The first statement in which they indicated they had been contemplating a change in their attitude was made on July 14, 1960, page 6311 of Hansard. The hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge) had this to say, and this was no doubt prior to the formation of the New Democratic party, but not long before. I quote from Hansard of that day when the hon. member said:
Western policy-
This was a statement of their policy at that time, the policy of his party.
Western policy is to balance NATO's weakness in conventional forces by being ready to use so-called tactical nuclear weapons. This idea is based on two false premises: first, that a weak force armed with nuclear weapons is going to beat the large force armed with nuclear weapons; second, that a nuclear war in Europe could possibly remain limited.
I am not quarrelling at the moment with the validity or otherwise of these premises. They might be valid. Then, the hon. member continued as follows:
Canada must insist that NATO recast its strategy, its tactics and its organization so that its defensive forces are capable of meeting any Soviet aggression with conventional weapons long enough-
I certainly agree with this.
-to allow diplomacy to seek a settlement before, progressively, tactical nuclear weapons and thermonuclear weapons are used.
In other words, according to the hon. gentleman who was the spokesman for his party at that time, NATO should have sufficient conventional strength in order to hold an attack until the forces of political negotiation and diplomacy could at least get working. If they were not successful, and if the attack continued on a scale which would be enlarged, as it probably would be, then according to this statement NATO would progressively be permitted to use tactical nuclear weapons and thermonuclear weapons.
Then, the hon. member for Kootenay West went on to say this:
We say that we should make it very clear to our NATO allies that we will withdraw from the alliance-
On what condition?
-unless they all honestly strive to give effect to disarmament and disengagement. The whole idea is to work toward the creation of a buffer zone in Europe at the same time as we make a buffer zone of Canada. That is our approach to this problem at the present time.
This represented I believe, Mr. Speaker, a very substantial change on the part of the C.C.F. party of that day. It was a move in the direction of the policy which was adopted at the founding conference of the New Democratic party. It is a policy towards NATO
The Address-Mr. Pearson to which we on this side took exception, and will continue to take exception as a policy which would end NATO. We are not willing, on this side, to do anything to weaken let alone destroy NATO.
My hon. friend, the leader of the New Democratic party, will recall that at that founding conference-I have not got the resolution before me but he will correct me if I misinterpret it-it was made quite clear that if NATO itself became a nuclear power, and NATO had already indicated in 1957 its requirement for nuclear protection, then Canada should withdraw as a member of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. They went further. They said that Canada should work towards-I have not the exact words but I think I am right in saying this, the abandonment of the NATO pact and the Warsaw pact. We should get rid of them both. I think that was the resolution adopted by the founding convention of his party. To that, we on this side take strong exception and we interpret this particular subamendment in the light of the resolution of the founding convention of his party on this subject.
There could be no greater triumph, Mr. Speaker, for the forces of imperial communism than to have the abandonment of both the NATO and Warsaw pacts. When I say that, I am not for one moment suggesting, as my hon. friend tried to suggest I was suggesting, that he and his friends are deliberately supporting in any way any communist objective. His interpretation of what I said during the election campaign, as I hope to point out, is quite false. The abandonment of the NATO pact would mean the abandonment of western collective security, the abandonment of a coalition of free states bound together in freedom to defend their security and thereby preserve the peace by showing their resolutions to defend their security. The abandonment of the Warsaw pact would be nothing at all because the Warsaw pact is a fagade. Who could say for one moment that if there were no Warsaw pact Soviet control over European communist satellites would be weakened in any way, shape or form? This is the part of the New Democratic policy in regard to NATO to which we take very strong exception indeed, and we relate that policy to the subamendment which is now before us.
The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) said this morning that I have stated, though he did not identify the statement in any way, that nuclear arms was not an issue. I did not know what he was talking about when he made that statement. Certainly, in the election campaign the acquisition of nuclear ammunition for those nuclear defensive arms systems which had been acquired

The Address-Mr. Pearson previously was indeed an issue. We accepted it as such. We made our position clear in regard to the matter and we stood on that position before the people in an election. Indeed, my hon. friend and his followers took a definite position on that matter also.
Then, the hon. gentleman went on to say that the leader of the Liberal party, and I took down what he said so I think it is correct, said that those of us who were opposing nuclear arms were seeking to promote the first objective of Soviet policy. I would ask him to give any evidence to support that kind of statement which he said, if it had been made, was a contemptible statement. If it had been made, it would have been a contemptible statement, but it was not made.

Their defence policy therefore, is not only against all nuclear weapons in Canada in the alliance, however defence in character, but it would destroy the alliance itself and weaken the security arrangements which are, in present circumstances, essential for peace.

If that is not a policy leading to the break-up of NATO, I would like to know what is.

I am not denying for one minute that the policy of the N.D.P., in its founding resolutions, would lead to the breakup of the North Atlantic Treaty Organization. Of course they would, and I would hope that perhaps the leader of that party, who may not hold these views or may have changed them since the founding convention, would make it clear it is not the policy of his party to break up NATO by refusing to be a member of that organization if it becomes a nuclear organization, which in fact it has been since 1957. I would also hope my hon. friend would repudiate the suggestion that we should work towards the abandonment of both the Warsaw pact and the NATO pact as being on the same level of interest to Canada in its determination to protect peace and security. It would be a very important gesture of clarification if my hon. friend, or one of his colleagues, would do that.
This morning the hon. gentleman made a very strong attack on the government, saying we had flouted parliamentary responsibility in not giving parliament a chance to decide on this matter before any decision was taken by the government. Well, Mr. Speaker, the proper constitutional position on this matter, which I have already repeated this afternoon, was put on the record by me last night, in the language of the former prime minister which he used some years ago, and which I need not repeat this afternoon.
Our position on this matter, as I have already said, was made clear during the election campaign. The N.D.P. position was made clear during the election campaign. Also the position of the Conservative party was made clear during that campaign, and that was to do nothing and wait and see what would turn up. Our position today in this parliament is that we are standing in the

face of this subamendment on that position, and this is surely the proper constitutional position for a government to take.
As I said yesterday, we are at the moment negotiating a bilateral agreement. If it is not a satisfactory agreement we will not accept it. We hope there will be a satisfactory bilateral agreement with the United States, which must be agreed on before any other step can be taken with regard to the acquisition of nuclear ammunition for the Canadian weapons system.
As is common to all the agreements that have been made by the United States with all other NATO members, the United States will retain custody of any nuclear warheads which are made available to the Canadian weapons system, but there will be joint control so that warheads which would be ready for instant use in the awful emergency of war, after release by the United States in that emergency, can be used only on orders from Canada itself. This is known, of course, as the two-key system and is common to all agreements for joint control of nuclear weapons, made by the United States with any NATO member.
This bilateral, political agreement, which is only one step, cannot in any event be completed before parliament has had a chance to express its views on this whole question of nuclear warheads for Canadian weapons. The hon. gentleman criticized me for making the statement the other day that no formal parliamentary approval was necessary. That of course is perfectly true in the sense that no formal parliamentary approval is necessary for this kind of agreement between two countries, unless that agreement takes a formal character in the shape of a treaty or an agreement which has to be ratified, and submitted to parliament for approval before ratification.
This is not that kind of agreement; but we are giving parliament an opportunity to express itself on this question and that is why a paragraph was put in the speech from the throne, and the hon. gentleman quite correctly has seized on that paragraph as a justification for his subamendment; and if the subamendment had not been made in those terms, we would be bringing forward very shortly a resolution to set up a defence committee to discuss defence policy. The question of nuclear arms can be discussed then, and if the verdict of parliament is against the government on this matter, if the verdict of parliament is even in favour of the subamendment, then parliament will have decided, the government will have been defeated, and if that is not a proper constitutional position to take then I
The Address-Mr. Pearson misread my constitutional history. If that is contempt of parliament I do not know what to say.
I would also point out to my hon. friend that parliament was called at the very earliest possible date so that it would have a chance to discuss and decide on this and any other matter. There was not one day's delay before parliament was called together. I would suggest to my hon. friend that the procedure adopted by the government in this matter satisfies, in spirit and in letter, the requirements that I mentioned in my speech of January 18 in Toronto, which my hon. friend himself quoted this morning.
Then the hon. gentleman said, and this has been repeated both by himself and others, that if we make this kind of agreement with the United States, and if this agreement is followed up by the technical arrangements which have to be negotiated to ensure the nuclear warheads will be available, under United States custody, for Canadian weapon systems in an emergency, then Canada will become a member of the nuclear club.
I would point out in that respect, Mr. Speaker, that the former prime minister on July 14, 1960 had something to say about this, and what he said seems to me to be very sensible and correct. He said at that time, as reported in Hansard at page 6271:
Mr. Speaker, it is a well known fact that United States law requires that the ownership of nuclear weapons must remain with the United States and that the use of such weapons requires presidential authorization. That is the law as it now stands and as it has been in effect since 1945 or 1946.
At the same time, as I have said before in the house, if and when nuclear weapons are acquired by the Canadian forces, these weapons will not be used except as the Canadian government decides and in the manner approved by the Canadian government. These two elements together constitute joint control, and joint control is consistent with the view I expressed in the house on February 20,
1959,	that it is important to limit the spread of nuclear weapons at the independent disposal of national governments.
If joint control is desirable in order to prevent the extension of nuclear weapons under the control of national governments, because if a national government has control of nuclear weapons that would indeed be an extension of the nuclear club, surely it is even more desirable to have as broad a based control as is possible under NATO so there will be additional safeguards to the use of these weapons and there will be additional obstacles against their extension under national control inside the NATO coalition. The former minister of national defence also had something to say about this on August 5,
1960,	when, as reported in Hansard on page 7652 he said:
So whether these warheads are placed in Canada or in the leased bases in Canada or in the United

Mr. Pearson Kingdom, the United States still retain possession of them until such time as the President of the United States releases them for use to the authorities of the country concerned.
That surely makes it clear that in the eyes of the recent government and in the eyes of the present government the provisions we are seeking for joint control of these weapons as long as these weapons are in the hands of Canadian forces, the provision for this kind of control to be brought under the authority of NATO to the greatest extent possible, is not putting Canada into the nuclear club and will not be interpreted by other countries as doing so. I ask the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), if he doubts that, whether he considers that those members of NATO who already have nuclear agreements with the United States are members of the nuclear club- Turkey, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Germany and perhaps one or two others. Is Germany a member of the nuclear club? The position of Canada, if these negotiations are satisfactorily concluded, will be exactly the same as the position of those other members of NATO who have made agreements and acted on them. Therefore, it is perfectly consistent to maintain that position while doing all we can-and we shall do all we can-to prevent the extension of the national manufacture and national custody or control of nuclear weapons.

I do not recall making any such statement in those terms. I am stating the position now as I know it to be in the light of all the information I have secured, including some information which was not available to us when we were in opposition and which reinforces the position we take on this matter.
The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) says that Canada has no commitment, or that he cannot find any commitment which requires such a decision as we have taken in order that it might be implemented. The hon. gentleman in his interesting speech quotes General Gerhart In support of that point of view and says Canada was not committed to nuclear arms under NORAD. Of course, it is perfectly true that when Canada under the previous government agreed to the establishment of NORAD there was no commitment of any kind regarding nuclear weapons, because the Canadian contribution to NORAD at that time was the Canadian


Arrow airplane. It was only subsequent to the destruction without trace of the Arrow and the acceptance by the previous government of the Bomarc missile that Canada accepted a nuclear commitment, because that missile, as the former prime ministar has pointed out so many times, cannot be effectively used without nuclear warheads.

speechtext: Could the Arrow?

speechtext:
Indeed, the Arrow could, and when the Arrow was constructed it was not suggested by those in charge at that time that the Arrow should carry nuclear weapons at all. But the prime minister of the day said, as will be found on page 1223 of Hansard of February 20, 1959, that the full potential of these defensive weapons is achieved only when they are armed with nuclear warheads -the Bomarc, the F-104, the Honest John and the Voodoo. He went on in the same speech to say-and I ask the house whether this is a commitment or not:
It is our intention to provide Canadian forces with modern and efficient weapons to enable them to fulfil their respective roles.
And these roles, as the former prime minister stated at the time, could not be effectively fulfilled without the nuclear warhead. In the same speech, to make this point doubly sure, the prime minister of that day said:
We must reluctantly admit the need in present circumstances for nuclear weapons of a defensive character.
Therefore, I ask the hon. gentleman if, having accepted this role, certain consequences do not automatically follow. When you accept a role you accept a commitment to undertake that role effectively. Having accepted the role, did not the previous government accept a commitment to acquire the ammunition without which these weapons systems would not be effective?
This is not a commitment put in the form of a treaty. It is not a commitment put in the shape of a formal agreement between two governments for ratification. But it is a moral and political commitment if any government ever made such a commitment to any other government.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: May I ask the right hon. gentleman a question? Did the Prime Minister think Canada had a commitment when he made his speech to students at Saskatchewan university on November 28 and said he was opposed to Canada accepting nuclear weapons?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I have that clipping from a university question and answer period to which the hon. member has referred and to which he also referred this morning. He did not read all of this article and, of course, what

he read was not in quotation marks. Oh, yes. I see it is in quotation marks. I said this, also in quotes:
Canada's NATO defence commitments are such that they cannot be discharged without nuclear weapons.
That is what I told the students. I will read on. This is also in quotation marks:
When these commitments were introduced, the Liberal party opposed them, not because of disagreement with the notion of collective defence, but because we felt it was the wrong role for Canada to play. Now we must either discharge our commitments or change them.
That, Mr. Speaker, is our position. The weapons systems are there. We learned last autumn that delivery of the F-104s was taking place-that the airplanes would in a few months be in Europe in the hands of the squadron. The Honest John missiles were in the hands of the regiments. The Bomarcs were on site at North Bay. At that time there was no possibility of changing this role without scrapping a billion dollars worth of equipment. Canada had to follow through until those roles were changed, and this government intends to do just that.
At that time, last autumn, we learned what could happen when you accept certain responsibilities. We learned from the Cuban crisis what the acceptance of certain commitments and responsibilities can do to our relations with our neighbour and our friend and we also learned last autumn over at the NATO meeting what the refusal of the government of that day either to alter the role they had undertaken or to follow through had done to our reputation in the NATO alliance. If the hon. gentleman in the face of all this evidence does not believe that some commitment was accepted by Canada, will he explain why the former minister of national defence and other ministers of the previous government resigned from that government? Was it not because the commitment was not being carried out?
Hon. members on the other side may now say there was no commitment, but they will not get support from at least one member of the front bench opposite in that regard. Therefore, it is clear the government cannot support the subamendment moved by the hon. gentleman. The subamendment says:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have Indicated their intention of acquiring nuclear arms for Canadian forces-
What we have indicated our intention of doing is to negotiate, if possible, a satisfactory bilateral agreement of the type negotiated between the United States and other NATO members and, if a satisfactory agreement providing for joint control can be reached, to proceed then with the technical
The Address-Mr. Pearson arrangements which will make it possible, not to acquire nuclear arms but to acquire the nuclear warheads for the arms systems which have already been obtained and which cannot be used effectively without them. And we propose to do this in a manner which will not prevent in any way the fight for disarmament in which this government will participate to the best of its ability. The first form of disarmament we must seek is nuclear disarmament, and the first form of that is the abolition of all testing. It is possible for the government to adopt this policy, until our role and commitments are changed as a result of defence reviews, without weakening in any single respect our fight for disarmament and for peace and security in the world. Thus I think the terms of the subamendment, particularly the expression "acquiring nuclear arms" are not accurate.
Then the subamendment goes on to say:
-thereby lessening the chances for nuclear disarmament and increasing the danger of nuclear war.
If the decision taken by the government to proceed in the direction I have indicated, along with other NATO members, is lessening the chances for nuclear disarmament and increasing the danger of nuclear war, then the implication of the criticism made by the hon. gentleman and his group is that we should withdraw from NATO, because the NATO alliance is now committed to a nuclear tactical deterrent. I do not believe for a minute that the nuclear tactical deterrent in the hands of the NATO council lessens the chances for nuclear disarmament or increases the danger of nuclear war. I think that until we can reach a general disarmament agreement, or some easing of tension which will allow a reduction of nuclear strength among those powers which now have it, there is no alternative open to the alliance but to make it conventionally strong in order to meet the first shock of an attack and then to build up a collective tactical deterrent should that conventional strength not be successful in holding the first attack. That seems to me to be a sensible defence policy and one which does not lessen the chances for nuclear disarmament or increase the danger of nuclear war. For these reasons we shall not be able to support the subamendment.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should like the Prime Minister to clarify the thinking of one poor layman on this complicated subject. The right hon. gentleman has talked about commitments. He has talked also about negotiating. He used the expression "if we can negotiate an agreement". Are we committed before we negotiate an agreement or after we have negotiated it? If we cannot negotiate an agreement, what about the commitment?

The Address-Mr. Pearson

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I should like to do everything I can to clarify the rarely bewildered mind of my poor layman friend. Surely, the hon. gentleman must know that when a government undertakes for its country a certain role in collective defence it also undertakes to adopt the means necessary to carry out that role. Otherwise, what is the point of accepting that role? You deceive your own people and you deceive the allies who rely on you to carry out that role. I am thinking, now, about the air division. Once we undertook the strike reconnaissance role for the F-104 aircraft we undertook to be effective in that role. That cannot be done without the acquisition of nuclear warheads. Having undertaken the role, the government of the day also undertook to negotiate an arrangement to that end with the United States. Indeed, it had begun negotiations for that purpose, thereby indicating it had accepted that commitment, too. But it did not follow through with those negotiations. We propose to do so.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I wonder if I may ask a brief question. In view of the fact that Denmark and Norway have not accepted nuclear weapons under NATO, does the Prime Minister consider that they, too, ought to withdraw from NATO?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: I do not for one minute. The Danish and Norwegian position was made clear at the beginning. They did not wish to participate in any form of collective nuclear defence under NATO. They did not wish to acquire nuclear warheads for any of their weapons and they did not wish to have the nuclear weapons of any other member of NATO on their soil. They made that perfectly clear. They also accepted the resolution of December 17, 1957, concerning the necessity of NATO itself building up a nuclear deterrent force. However, they said from the beginning they did not wish to be involved in its implementation. Their decision was clear and it is respected. That is a very different situation from the one in which Canada finds itself at the present time.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: About these commitments by Canada. Can the Prime Minister tell us at what level they were taken? Was it at cabinet level or at military staff level?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The government of the day should answer that question. But the former prime minister spoke to the house on his return from a NATO council meeting and the minister of national defence also spoke to the house later indicating the new kind of strike reconnaissance role which had been undertaken. Therefore, the commitments were undertaken at the appropriate level, which was the level of the government of the day.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: But those commitments were not endorsed by parliament.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: They were brought before the House of Commons and the government was not defeated in the debate which followed the making of those commitments. Therefore, they were endorsed by the house.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on entering this debate for the first time I should like to convey through you, Mr. Deputy Speaker, to the Speaker of the house my congratulations on his appointment to an office for which he is eminently suited by training, character and disposition. I should like to wish him well in the performance of his duties.
I should also at this stage express my congratulations to the mover and the seconder of this address who capably performed a rather difficult task, as is recognized by all of those who have preceded them in entering the House of Commons. I hope they continue to have success in their deliberations here.
I had not intended, Mr. Speaker, entering into the debate on this particular subject at this time, but it is an interesting topic and I should like to deal with some of the remarks which have been made. I take note of the fact that this morning the leader of the New Democratic party was as bold as a lion in presenting a case against the government, whereas the night before he had been very mild indeed, talking about no need for another election, and echoing the sentiments of the leader of the Social Credit party about it being urgent now for people to get down to business, that politics should be forgotten, and that a non-partisan approach should be taken to these various subjects. I do not see how you can have non-partisan approaches where political parties have divergent opinions on so many matters. The leader of the New Democratic party softened his attack when he finally came to move his amendment, with which I shall deal later on.
We have just listened with some interest but not much enlightenment to the remarks of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson). Yesterday he was talking about the building up of straw men and knocking them over. This is a field in which he is adept. Today he built up a straw man. He said that the dissatisfaction with the amendment moved by the New Democratic party was dependant upon an attitude taken by that party at some convention, or on another occasion, with regard to NATO. The amendment has nothing, to do, as I see it, with NATO; it has something to do with the announced policy of the present government, but the Prime Minister

spent a great deal of time talking about the New Democratic party and its general attitude. It was for that reason he said, that he could not accept the amendment.
We might suggest that the subamendment should be accepted by the government for the very reason that in days gone by the Liberal party time and again expressed itself quite forcefully against any extension of the nuclear club, against any extension of the use of atomic weapons, and was quite clear that there should be no nuclear weapons on Canadian soil. I think that now the Liberal party would find itself in agreement with this amendment in view of its past history.
Of course, a most remarkable change took place during the parliamentary recess last December-January. The leader of the New Democratic party asked the present Prime Minister where he had been during that recess, whom he had seen, to whom he had talked, from whom he had taken his instructions, and I would repeat those questions to which we have not had an answer. Something happened in the interval, and the reversal of a position taken occurred early in January.
In addition to building up a straw man concerning the policy of the New Democratic party, the Prime Minister also referred at some considerable length to the decision of the North Atlantic council in December 1957. He said that the parliament of that day raised no objection. I might remind him that there was no indication in that decision that Canadian forces would be using nuclear weapons or that nuclear weapons would be stored on Canadian soil. The North Atlantic council decided-and I read from the communique of that period-the following:
NATO should establish stocks of nuclear warheads which will be readily available for the defence of the alliance in case of need.
The NATO council decided to accept an offer by the United States government under which that government-
-would deploy nuclear warheads under United States custody in accordance with NATO defensive planning in an agreement with the nations directly concerned. In the event of hostilities nuclear warheads would be released to the appropriate NATO supreme allied commander for employment by nuclear capable forces.
There was agreement by Canada to that general policy on the part of NATO in order to bolster up the weak conventional forces of that day; but there was no obligation, intention or desire on the part of Canada to play any part in that nuclear deterrent force; and in any case the weapons were all held by the United States. So I fail to see what relationship there is between the situation at the present moment and that prevailing in 1957 when the Prime Minister attempts to make
The Address-Mr. Churchill out that the parliament of that day raised no objection to the NATO policy as announced in that year.
The main attack launched this morning by the leader of the New Democratic party was on the flouting of parliament, on the disregard of parliament by the present government, on the contempt for parliament shown by the present government. He made his case on the fact that the Prime Minister had announced that Canada was going to go ahead with providing nuclear weapons for her forces and was going to have nuclear weapons placed on Canadian soil. It was to this that the leader of the New Democratic party objected. He said that this was not correct. He said: "You, the government, have not received a mandate from the people to take any such action as this. Nor have you received a mandate here in parliament. You do not know whether you are acceptable to parliament as the government of this country. You have been taking action without authority". It was on that basis that the amendment was drawn.
My expectation had been that when the amendment was read out, after the word "intention" the phrase "without consulting parliament" would have appeared. The amendment would then have read:
We regret that Your Excellency's advisers have indicated their intention without consulting parliament of acquiring nuclear arms for Canadian forces-
-and so on. That was the sum and substance of the speech made by the leader of the New Democratic party-the lack of authority in the hands of the present government, no mandate from the people to do this, no authority from this parliament to take any such action whatsoever.
I find it very difficult to follow the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) in his convolutions, ramifications and wanderings with regard to this particular question. Even in the speech from the throne, where there was a chance for clarity of expression after an election campaign when nuclear arms were discussed on every platform in the country, all that this government could come up with was the following phrase:
The armed forces of Canada should have available the modern weapons necessary to perform effectively the defensive tasks which Canada has undertaken in the alliance.
Why should the Prime Minister and his colleagues not have put in clear and distinct words what they mean by "modern weapons"?

speechtext:
The F-104.

The Address-Mr. Churchill

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Do they mean weapons with nuclear tips? Do they mean nuclear warheads? They are just being evasive. They are afraid to set it out clearly and distinctly so that everybody can understand. I think one can say that our forces have modern weapons right now to perform effectively their defensive tasks. It depends on what the defensive task is and so far our armed forces are prepared for those tasks. There was no clarity there at all.
I noted that the speech the right hon. gentleman made yesterday was filled with many ifs and buts and other qualifications. He is speaking about the NATO council meeting and he says, as found on page 63 of Hansard:
It is quite clear from the nature of this meeting that there will be no discussion, let alone any recommendation, about the actual role undertaken by any member of the alliance.
Just two paragraphs later he says:
It may well be that at the NATO council meeting there may be a recommendation that the defence policy of the coalition should be re-examined. I would hope that could be done-
On the one hand, he says it is quite clear that there will be no discussion or recommendation about the role of any member and then he immediately goes on to say that there may be a recommendation with regard to the role or defence policy of the coalition. He then expresses the hope that there will be, and I presume he has given instructions to the delegation representing Canada at the NATO meeting to raise that question. Then he goes on to say, and he repeated it this afternoon- -just as Canada's defence policy will be reexamined in this house and by a special committee of this house.
I wonder what that will amount to? This is a great sop thrown to parliament. A defence committee on policy-I am not sure they have said it will be on policy-will be appointed. If it is a defence committee on policy the purpose is to give the government a chance to evade its responsibility. Time and time again we heard last year from members who now sit on the treasury benches that it was the duty of a government to make a decision and get on with the job. Here you have an ineffective, uncertain, poorly organized government not sure of its position saying: We do not know what we should do about defence policy so we will set up a committee of parliament to give us its opinion.
Why not set up a committee to determine the budget for parliament? That would be a nice, non-partisan interparty committee to determine the economic future of Canada. Is the government not prepared to make a definite statement of policy with regard to our economic conditions, with regard to taxation

and things of that nature? I think perhaps it is; but on defence, oh, no. This is a very touchy subject, so we must all get together and get the government off the hook.
I call upon the government to come out clearly, decisively and with frankness and say just what its policy is because it is not disclosed in the speech we heard yesterday by the Prime Minister or in what he said this afternoon. He went on to say yesterday with regard to the NATO meeting:
The only question that will arise here is whether those forces will be under a separate NATO nuclear command; whether the R.C.A.F.-
Then he puts in an if clause again.
-if it discharges the nuclear role accepted for it, should continue its present position in the NATO command or whether it should be under a separate NATO nuclear command organization.
Why is there some suggestion of doubt whether the R.C.A.F. will discharge the nuclear role accepted for it? The if is there. There is an escape hatch, a way out for a person who has spent quite a bit of his lifetime working out means of evading issues and skirting around problems.
The Prime Minister was at great pains to point out that last autumn the problem was clear, that members of the Liberal party found out that Canada was not, as he put it, living up to her commitments. He has not defined those commitments. He is still searching to see what commitments there are, if any, but he said last fall that they had found out that the delivery of Starfighters was taking place in Europe. I ask the Prime Minister: What Starfighters were delivered in Europe last fall? How many? How many are now there ready for action? How many were ready in the middle of April this year?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: He does not know.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Not one, because they need ammunition.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY

The present Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) does not know or did not know last winter. Only one squadron of 18 planes was ready by the middle of April of this year, and yet members of the Liberal party have been talking for the last several months about the air division in Europe being unarmed. The air division in Europe does not consist of Starfighters yet. It is being reorganized so that it will be equipped with Starfighters, and only one squadron, 18 planes, was ready by the middle of April and it will not be fully trained for active service until some time in June. Those are the facts.
Why did the people who made these great discoveries last fall not tell us and tell the people of Canada what they had discovered?

They discovered last fall that the Starfighters were only in the process of being sent over to Europe, that they had to be modified to a very great extent after they reached there and that only one squadron was to be ready by the middle of April.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Political purposes.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Prime Minister interrupted and said there was no ammunition for them. They have created the impression that we have 144 planes flying around in Europe unarmed. Not at all. Only 18 of them were ready by the middle of April. When the time comes to arm them, are they going to be flying around with nuclear bombs attached to their undercarriages? Are they going to try practice shots with these nuclear weapons? This morning I asked a question of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) with regard to the Honest John rocket battery. We had bogus information spread by the Liberal party for several months to the effect the Honest John artillery battery was sitting over in Europe unarmed, not ready for action. They said that the missile on board the rocket discharger had sand in the warhead. Well, it is not sand, it is concrete and it is there for a purpose.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill) laughs, but he laughs from ignorance. This concrete is there for a purpose. In order to obtain the equivalent weight of the live warhead on the missile that will be used in wartime, this concrete filled warhead has been attached. This enables the troops to get their full training short of discharging a nuclear weapon. They have a missile of the same length, the same size and same weight as they would use in wartime. Would you have this battery of artillery travelling about Europe with nuclear warheads on board? What if somebody pushed the trigger by mistake? Of course, it is all nonsense. These weapons will not have nuclear warheads attached to them until the alert has been sounded and war is imminent.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: You have no agreement with the United States to make that possible.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: The Honest John artillery battery is only a 20-minute drive away from the missile storage dump and when an alert is sounded they could be ready to be deployed within two hours.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader

speechtext:
They come under the British division which has charge of the missile dump. If war broke out the missiles would
The Address-Mr. Churchill be provided for the Honest John battery. Here, we have been given the false information that this battery is over there, that it is useless, and so on. This is not true. The battery is well trained. I saw it and I saw the missile dump. They could go into action in under two hours fully armed with atomic warheads. It would be simply ridiculous to have these atomic warheads attached now and in the hands of troops who would be used on manoeuvres. You certainly do not take practice shots with atomic warheads.
I asked the Minister of National Defence this morning if he were going to have the Honest John equipped with these nuclear warheads. He said that this matter was under consideration by the government and the decision would depend to a considerable extent on the outcome of negotiations now being carried on by his colleague the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). Well, he will not get much help from him. Why is the Minister of National Defence not taking part in these consultations?
This is the situation with regard to these matters. Furthermore, Mr. Speaker, when you talk about the Starfighter, the missile dump for the Starfighter at Zweibriicken was started in the wintertime and when I was there in February it was only partially completed. It will not be completed until June, so how can you arm Starfighters with atomic weapons when the missile dump has not been provided? My friends in the Liberal party have been misleading the public across this country by giving them false information concerning our air division in Europe and the availability of atomic missiles for that air division.
The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) talks about living up to our commitment. We have stated, and we state again, that we have met all our commitments. Let him produce a commitment that has not been met. On May 22, 1959, at a meeting of the NATO council, Mr. Dillon for the United States and Mr. Heeney for Canada signed an agreement for co-operation in the use of atomic energy for mutual defence purposes. This document was tabled in congress before being printed on July 14, 1959 and is listed as report No. 513 of the Senate of the United States, 86th congress, first session. I am sure that the Prime Minister would have this information available from that particular source. It is very familiar to him. In the days of the Eisenhower administration, there was no difficulty. President Eisenhower, in his letter of transmittal of this document to congress, wrote as follows:
These agreements will enable the United States to co-operate effectively in mutual defence planning

The Address-Mr. Churchill with these nations and in the training of their respective NATO forces in order that, if an attack on NATO should occur, under the direction of the Supreme Allied Commander for Europe these forces could effectively use nuclear weapons in their defence.
The essential part of this agreement between the two governments is to be found in article I which reads as follows:
Each party will communicate to and exchange with the other party, information and transfer materials and equipment to the other party.
Article II-exchange of information-each party will communicate to .or exchange with the other party such classified information as is jointly determined to be necessary to:
(B) The training of personnel in the employment of and defence against atomic weapons and other military applications of atomic energy.
Then, article VI reads:
Under this agreement there will be no transfer by either party of atomic weapons or non-nuclear parts of atomic weapons.
Atomic weapon is defined as any device utilizing atomic energy, the principal purpose of which is for use as a weapon. This is the extent of the agreement and it dates from 1959. We could have information, our troops would be trained in the use of those weapons, but under no circumstances would the United States allow these nuclear weapons to be transferred to the use of another country.
Here is the difficulty in which the Prime Minister finds himself. He talks airily about the United States having a finger on the trigger and Canada having a finger on the safety catch. He talks airily about joint control, the two-key system. Let us discover what he will come up with in his negotiations. He will find that strict control will be kept by the United States. As the Winnipeg Tribune put it in big headlines on May 16, "U.S. will guard nuclear warheads on Canadian soil". The Prime Minister said the nuclear storage points would have what he called an outside security guard of Canadian troops. Canadian troops will not be allowed within the compound; they will be kept outside. Not one nuclear weapon, if ever obtained, will be fired without the consent of the United States. The Canadians would simply be carriers or users under United States authority or control as the Winnipeg Tribune suggests. I quote from the editorial of May 16:
What he meant all along-
Referring to the present Prime Minister.
-on the "acceptance" of nuclear arms was the establishment on Canadian soil of American nuclear depots, under American control and custody.
