I should like first of all to congratulate you on your appointment to the office of chairman of committees of the house and of Deputy Speaker. I also extend my best wishes to Mr. Speaker himself.
I also wish to congratulate the mover and the seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne, as well as the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Lamontagne) who, by getting himself elected as member for Outremont-St. Jean, has accomplished the most remarkable feat of his career.
I should like to take this opportunity to speak about my riding of Quebec-Montmo-rency and to point out that in the 1962 election, there were 12 candidates, while in April 1963, there were at least nine. This shows that Quebec-Montmorency is somewhat active in the field of politics.
I also wish to say a few words about certain industries of my riding which are faced with difficulties at present. For instance, the shipyard of St. Laurent, on the island of Orleans, which can build various kinds of ships is on the point of closing down because certain contracts that it could carry out have not yet been passed.
There is also the case of the employees of Valcartier arsenals and of the C.A.R.D.E., who wonder whether they will keep their jobs long, in view of the present circumstances.
Certain postal employees also often make representations to me with regard to their working hours, salary rates as well as other difficulties they encounter.
Finally, I wish to say a few words about veterans, several of whom asked me if it would be possible to receive old age pensions at the age of 65, without any means test as well as an increase of their regular veterans' pensions.
We have heard earlier about the election campaign. Someone hinted that the party now in power had received certain amounts of money. It was said that it had carried out propaganda, which if it was not untrue, was at least rather remote from the truth.
I have here some newspaper clippings, one being from L'Action dated April 4, containing a Canadian Press dispatch, which I quote:
All parties, except the Liberals have reduced their publicity budgets.
Certain publicity methods have been employed which have elicited derogatory comments on the part of the very persons who were being quoted. I have here an article published in the Sherbrooke Tribune dated Wednesday, April 3, 1963, in which Father
The Address-Mr. Marcoux Bouvier denounces the use of his name and the opinions credited to him.
That is why I was very disappointed to learn that certain of my colleagues were throwing themselves wholeheartedly in the arms of people who had used such methods.
I should like now to comment on the international situation which seems to be in the foreground of the present time.
We should not forget that we are now living through and now witnessing a test of strength between east and west. It should not be forgotten also that the eastern group, ideologically speaking, is closely tied to its doctrine of atheistic materialism, while such is not the case with the western forces. So, I think we should identify ourselves a bit more with the anti-atheistic materialism doctrine by recognizing God as the object of our endeavours. Nor should we forget that the eastern powers use their economic system to make their ideology acceptable to underdeveloped countries.
As for us, we have always based our ideological policy on the restrictions imposed by our economic system. That is why Social Credit has constantly favoured an economic policy in keeping with the democratic system we wish to extend to all people on earth.
There is a lot of talk about nuclear weapons, to such an extent that the people of Canada, that of Quebec included, of which I am a representative, finally realize once again that the old-line parties are treating them with scorn most of the time and may change their mind. One wonders if it is not simply a question of taking over the government and of using arguments with which to win elections.
Most people today are inclined to believe that the question of nuclear arms is beyond discussion. There are some who are 100 per cent for, other who are 100 per cent against. It is said that the matter cannot be discussed. Be that as it may, it seems to me that we have here a complex problem the solution to which does not meet with unanimous approval.
Consequently, I should like to recall historical facts, the better to put ourselves in the picture, as I myself can see it.
At the end of what has been called the "Japanese war", the damages wrought by the atomic bomb were revealed to the public at large. The United States of America alone held the secret of atomic power. But Russia was not to remain far behind. With the assistance of spies, as the Gouzenko affair clearly revealed, they soon made up for lost

The Address-Mr. Marcoux time and perfected a bomb just as powerful as the one which was exploded over Hiroshima. Thus, a second giant was born which was a true match for the first one.
In the following years, the present Prime Minister used his influence to play a role which was later described as a mission of peace. At the time, he was trying to put across the following theory: The United States remained the great defenders of democracy. They were to increase their assistance to underdeveloped countries and, consequently, the American policy was the only one which could save the rest of the world from Soviet domination. That is still true today.
Then, in 1957, Canada gave a new direction to its foreign policy. Having never been too enthusiastic about the colonial powers and having never associated itself with capitalism, our aim was to take advantage of the situation and to stress the great prestige our country enjoyed considering its relatively small population to promote a policy of neutrality. Canada strived to convert the uncommitted countries of the world to form a group of neutral states which would stand up against the adoption of nuclear weapons.
While Castro fed Cuba to the Russian bear, Canada succeeded in winning the uncommitted countries to the idea of forming an association.
Thus, our country made quite a reputation for itself by its action among the new states, first to spread the American policy and then to unite the uncommitted countries for the maintenance of peace outside the sphere of influence of the two nuclear giants.
At the very moment when Canada was carrying on its work as a mediator, it decided to accept defensive nuclear weapons. Canada had to meet her obligations towards NORAD and NATO. Faced with this fact, the Canadian government had to make its decisions public, while safeguarding its interests as much as possible from the electoral point of view. With typical indecision, the Conservative government chose to remain on tne fence. The present Prime Minister expressed himself categorically. Canada should not become one day a nuclear power.
I have here the Liberal program of 1962 from which I shall quote a few excerpts:
For instance, Bomarc missiles are useless without nuclear warheads; on the other hand, their effectiveness is so doubtful that the previous government refused to equip them with such warheads. A new Liberal government would avoid

such indecision and such costly wastefulness. It will not venture into projects entailing heavy expenditures and abandon them later on by refusing to purchase the weapons they require.
That was the Liberal program of 1962, and here is what we find further on:
In the light of current data, the defence policy of a new Liberal government will not require Canada to become a nuclear power through the manufacture, acquisition or use of nuclear weapons, whether under Canadian or American control.
This is again the Liberal program of 1962, bearing the picture of the present Prime Minister.
The socialists have also stated clearly where they stand. I am not speaking of the party itself, but of socialism in general. They are positively against nuclear arms. They even suggest complete disarmament to the United States and, apparently, the same suggestion is to be made a little later on to the Soviet union. There is then no compromise possible as far as they are concerned. It was said earlier, of course, following the statement of the Prime Minister, that both groups should not be too closely identified.
I have here an excerpt from the March 20, 1963 issue of the Moncton Transcript, where I find the following:
(Text):
Leslie Morris, leader of the Canadian communist party, said Tuesday night that party members across the country are being urged to actively "support, work for and help finance" the campaigns of the New Democratic party candidates in the federal election campaign.
(Translation):
This is what is said further on:
(Text):
Mr. Morris said strong N.D.P. representation in parliament is the best guarantee that nuclear arms will not be brought into Canada.
(Translation):
I have here a statement made by Mr. Leslie Morris, secretary general of the Canadian communist party, where he says the following:
We beg of you, in the interests of peace and of our country, to vote in the House of Commons, against the adoption of nuclear arms.
And we know that the Canadian communist party is doing much more for other countries than for ours. Furthermore, in this statement, the rejection of nuclear arms is requested.
A great number of voters refused to accept the Liberal platform regarding nuclear arms, devotedly subservient to Kennedy.
And, finally it is said in that circular letter:
Peace, national security and the life of each one of us will be endangered if we accept Kennedy's nuclear plans.
This means, Mr. Speaker, that the situation is not as simple as we are led to believe.

The election takes place, the sessions run their course, and the government cannot explain clearly its defence policy. And then the present Prime Minister goes to the United States. We know what happened there. Apparently he met with General Norstad. Following that interview he seems to have suddenly reversed his policy. Canada, it seems, must have nuclear warheads. He seems to be prepared to play again the part of the United States' emissary, consisting precisely in advocating the policy of our friends to the south and to become the non-official spokesman of the state department, which itself considered not without interest the possibility that the non-committed group might come round to its policy.
Then came the dissolution of both houses following the amendment everyone knows about. The present Prime Minister condemns again the adoption of nuclear arms while insisting that our commitments towards the United States must be fulfilled. Obviously, it is an admission that, in spite of his opposition to nuclear arms, he wants Canada to acquire them.
Speaking of commitments reminds me, for instance, of parents who would have been foolish enough to give rifles to their children and who would be even more so, in my opinion, if they were to give them also bullets to put in them.
The stand I take, along with many thousands of people in Quebec, is a little difficult to state clearly because that question is made up of so many facts.
We must, more than ever, be ready to fight communism, whether on the military or the ideological level. And, at this stage, I am happy to note that the United States are strong enough to challenge the U.S.S.R. in the field of atomic weapons. We will, therefore, morally support that country in its determination to stop the spread of the communist dictatorship in the world.
But-because there is a but-when the former government, after rejecting the Avro-105 program, decided to acquire Bomarc missiles, the President of the United States announced that the Bomarc missiles were obsolete, that they did not constitute, in any way, an effective weapon to stop or destroy enemy missiles carrying bombs of several megatons, in short, that our present means of defence have no value, and that the only possible "alternative" remains pure and simple offensive, and that is what the United States are capable of doing, I would imagine.
In the light of those new facts, and when one thinks of the huge sums of money uselessly spent on a defence system as ineffective as it is obsolete, one can declare oneself
The Address-Mr. Marcoux against nuclear arms and even ready to fight against the acquisition of such weapons.
Obviously, our low money reserves cannot be wasted. On the contrary, we must use them wittingly in order to help Canada fight unemployment, invest money to fight unemployment and also to help the underdeveloped countries who are waiting for our assistance to throw themselves in our arms instead of seeking help from our enemies.
I do not want to speak longer on the question of nuclear arms. Nevertheless that explains, I think, the various positions taken by different groups. Moreover, I think that we must take everything into consideration before reaching a decision, whatever it is. In my opinion, we cannot settle this question by saying yes or no, as have already done certain irresponsible persons. We must be familiar with all the facts related to the question.
The speech from the throne also mentions the question of bilingualism and also, indirectly, that of biculturalism. In my opinion, before setting up a commission, maybe the government should start by giving the house completely bilingual stationery, whether it is for a French or an English speaking member. I am of the opinion that if all the Commons stationery was printed in both languages, that would be at least a relatively official acknowledgement of the intention that the French language is to be officially recognized.
And when one knows that the President of the Privy Council is the one that will see to the application of these measures, one is entitled to wonder, allowance being made for the past and all respect due to him, if he is still in favour of centralization and if he is still advocating the taxation equalization system he himself invented with the help of a few associates. It is necessary that the autonomy of all provinces be recognized at any price and that the taxation means they need be given back to them.
The speech from the throne mentions the creation of a sort of municipal development bank. Of course this measure, if it is enacted, it will have to take into account provincial rights and privileges. May I point out to the house that nowadays the provinces are less cramped by their lack of funds than by the interest they have to pay on borrowed money. I have here a newspaper article, which appeared in L'Evenement of Quebec

The Address-Mr. Marcoux on March 19, 1963; it states that in the sole province of Quebec, the debenture debt of municipalities amounts to $1 billion.
I think-as the Liberals themselves seemingly thought not so long ago-that only a debt-free money system can really help the municipal governments.
As for unemployment, we are not given too many details about what is going to be done in order to check it.
I remember that in 1958, the present President of the Privy Council, who tried desperately to put the Liberal party back into power, advocated a method which seems quite acceptable to the Social Credit party and which consists in a six-month period of fiscal exoneration which means that, during a period of six months, no taxes will be deducted at the source, as he said at that time, in order to give immediate purchasing power to the people, whereas public works can only be a long term solution.
Incidentally, I think that during the last election, the Liberals have shown that they did have a solution for the unemployment problem: it would be to hold an election for 12 months every year, because, during those campaigns they always had enough money at their disposal and employed very many people.
Another provision which would be very popular in some districts would be the elimination of receipts for charitable donations, which creates many difficulties when preparing income tax returns.
The speech from the throne refers to the redistribution of electoral districts. I hope that this task will be accomplished in a spirit of justice, and taking into account the various categories of citizens and social strata which are represented in this house.
Now, a brief reference to Labrador. I think that this territory should be given back to the province of Quebec. I know that this matter is the core of a very difficult issue. But for a government which claims it can do so much in 60 days of decision, it should be easy to give back to Quebec the Labrador territory which belongs to it.
I should also like to call the attention of the government to the fact that a certain form of socialism has crept into the civil service without its knowledge, I suppose. I received letters from employees of the Post Office Department saying that even in Russia, a treatment like the one experienced by those employees would not be tolerated. I suppose that some pressures could be exerted on the people concerned to make life a little easier for the post office employees. Someone even observed to me lately that some post office employees had enjoyed a holiday on the


Queen's birthday while some others were not allowed the same privilege. Surely, something is not working properly in that department.
I would like now to make a suggestion to the Minister of Justice (Mr. Chevrier). We are told that a new penitentiary will be built. It is obvious that the province of Quebec and other areas need penitentiaries because there are laws and there are people who break the law. Instead of building a large penitentiary I would suggest that one be erected in the Montreal area and another in the Quebec city area. I do not imply that we should only build some in the city of Montreal or Quebec but simply in the neighbourhood of both those cities in order to reduce the hardship of those who have to go there.
I hope that this minority government will show that it is prepared to accept suggestions from the opposition parties which, even though they are sitting across the aisle, may have some rational ideas. The whole nation hopes to get real action from this government.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, upon this occasion of my first speech delivered in this house I should like to congratulate you upon your elevation to your high office. I am sure that the voices of approval of so many hon. members on both sides of this house properly express the unanimity of opinion upon your appointment. I would also take this occasion to extend to the mover and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne congratulations on the fine jobs they have done.
I come from the historic constituency of Halifax, in the province of Nova Scotia, where we have some of the finest institutions of higher learning to be found in the nation. This is attested to by the fact that expatriate Nova Scotians have over the years held a disproportionate number of high positions in government, commerce and education, not only throughout this nation but also in the United States. My constituency comprises the cities of Dartmouth and Halifax, and the county of Halifax, with a total population in the vicinity of 225,000. Mr. Speaker, we are one of the two remaining dual constituencies in Canada, and I am proud to represent, along with my colleague, the fine people of that area. I might say, Mr. Speaker, that I am proud to be associated, in representing that constituency, with the mayor of Halifax, a man who has worked tirelessly and ably for the betterment of that city.

As a freshman member sitting on this side of the house I was greatly encouraged by the contents of the speech from the throne. Coming from an area which has contributed much to confederation but has never received a full share of prosperity from confederation, I was enormously encouraged by the expressed intention of this government to make the Atlantic development board a vital work force. The funds allocated to this board give it the potential to materially aid the economy of the Atlantic region. This is a vast improvement over the role in which the previous administration had cast this body. The former government made it only an advisory board without funds, capable only of making recommendations to the government, a role which the Atlantic provinces economic council, informally at least, was carrying out already along with its other duties, and doing so with personnel at least equally able. I was pleased to see recognition in the speech from the throne of unemployment as a problem which must be faced. Under the former administration there was an unwillingness to admit that unemployment was an existing problem. I was also pleased to notice the intention to establish a department of industry with an area development agency, because this is of great importance to Nova Scotia. I am confident that this government will use these tools to improve the economic level of the maritime provinces.
There seems today to be a new willingness across the country to recognize the need for special measures to aid the development of areas which have lagged in industrial growth for one or more reasons. Nova Scotia is such an area. As Nova Scotians, we are proud to be part of confederation; but never let it be forgotten that Nova Scotia has suffered much because of confederation. Our national trade lines have been altered and indeed obliterated by the tariff policies which were necessary to develop industry in central Canada. In my constituency, despite disadvantages we have made great strides. We have grown in size and enterprise to the point that we have created an immediate market which will attract and which has attracted many companies to establish plants to serve this market.
One of the principal cornerstones of our progress has been the existence as a vital part of our economy of the port of Halifax. The largest industry of our constituency has since the building of the railway link with Quebec and Ontario shortly after confederation been our port business in the role of handling goods shipped from or to central Canada, in the winter months. Indeed, the establishment of Halifax as a national winter port for this purpose was one of the main
The Address-Mr. Regan considerations which enticed Nova Scotia to come into confederation. This historic role of Halifax as a national winter port was recognized by the federal government many years ago in the establishment of extensive port facilities.
However, Mr. Speaker, successive freight rate increases since world war II, the use of American ports to ship Canadian goods and the ever-increasing volume of winter traffic on the St. Lawrence has adversely affected our port business, so that despite the natural growth of Canada our total import and export tonnage in the port of Halifax has been static or has decreased during the past six years. The competitive position of the port of Halifax has been upset by the new and large subsidies given to competitive areas in recent years. It is true that these subsidies were of an indirect type. The building of the St. Lawrence seaway was such a subsidy to the lake ports. The use of ice-breakers each at a cost of $13,000 a day, just to operate, on the St. Lawrence to lengthen the shipping season to Montreal is a new subsidy for the port of Montreal. Dredging at federal government expense in the St. Lawrence is yet another subsidy to the St. Lawrence.
(Translation):
In Nova Scotia, Mr. Speaker, we follow with interest and we admire and approve the desires of the people of Quebec to improve their situation in the confederation. We always support movements in this direction.
Nevertheless, I am sure that the representatives of this great province, who sit on both sides of the house, will recognize that Nova Scotia has been even less favoured by this same confederation.
Like all Canadians, Mr. Speaker, they acknowledge the need for regional development and they know that Nova Scotia needs help for its development because of the disadvantages of its geographical situation.
Therefore, I am sure that all Canadians will support a review of railway rates so that the Halifax harbour may remain competitive considering the development of winter navigation on the St. Lawrence river.
I am confident that the trade expansion of Canada will permit to increase the volume of shipping so as to make full use of the port facilities of the maritime provinces and on the St. Lawrence.
That is why, Mr. Speaker, I am calling for the recognition of the vital importance of winter shipping for Halifax.
(Text):
After hearing Halifax French, Mr. Speaker, there may be some question whether my colleagues of the French language still want people in other parts of Canada to attempt

The Address-Mr. Regan to speak it. In these days of giant government deficits perhaps our nation should fully utilize the port facilities readily available for winter shipping rather than spend vast sums to clear ports normally clogged by ice in the winter months. Perhaps this is an unnecessary expense causing our national investment in winter port facilities to be wasted and not used.
We have in Halifax the best year-round, natural, deep-water, ice-free port in the world. The finest port facilities have been established there and it is indeed false economy to abandon this winter port, giving rise to the need of some form of vast new federal aid to our area when we can move toward prosperity on our own, through full utilization of our port.
But, Mr. Speaker, we know that progress cannot be stopped, and if there is to be winter navigation on the St. Lawrence then I am sure that all hon. members will agree that we must have a new look at the railway freight rates applicable to goods imported or exported through maritime ports. I would urge the Minister of Transport (Mr. Mcll-raith) to establish a commission to investigate the effect of the seaway and of winter navigation in the St. Lawrence on the economy of the maritimes. I would expect that such a commission would revise the applicable freight rates to restore the competitive position of our port, because if that competitive position is restored we in Halifax with our ice-free port are willing to meet competition at any time. For every dollar spent by way of new subsidy to our competitors along the St. Lawrence, let us see a dollar spent by way of transportation subsidy on goods being shipped to or from Halifax.
I should like to say a word or two, Mr. Speaker, with regard to the recently announced pay increases and other improvements for the men of the armed forces. Canada has been able to build an effective volunteer army, navy and air force in the past by offering to the young men of our nation a career in the services which was attractive. It has managed to retain them in the forces by keeping conditions attractive. It has thus kept their morale high. This, many feel, has been far more satisfactory than a system of peacetime conscription but if we are to have our present system we must pay for it. Naturally we must continue to make service life attractive to our young people.
For this reason and because pay increases and other adjustments for our servicemen were long overdue, I hail this government measure as one of the real accomplishments of the first 60 days. These improvements

were long overdue. The previous administration had neglected the men of the forces and had thus started to affect the morale of many servicemen.
Coming from the constituency which contains the principal base of the Royal Canadian Navy, I particularly want to say on behalf of the men of the navy that this was a step in the right direction. I am confident that under the able direction of the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer) the navy will be equipped with the best and most modern weapons and that the welfare of the servicemen will at all times be considered. While I am a member of this honourable house I will, whenever the occasion presents itself during consideration of any matter relevant to the navy, stand with pride and say that I speak for the men of the navy.
A very large amount of my practice as a lawyer, Mr. Speaker, has been devoted to management-labour relations and I have had the privilege, in conciliation, arbitration, certification and in court matters, to act for many of the large unions of our nation. As one who has been very close to and very interested in the welfare of the working man, I want to say that I am extremely grateful for the support which many trade unionists gave me in the recent election. I think they too will find much in the speech from the throne which will increase their support for the new administration. After six years in which many of their problems were neglected and during which the government of the day refused to recognize unemployment as a problem, I feel that we are in for a wholesome and welcome change. I said earlier that the new government in the throne speech has already recognized unemployment as a problem, and I want to say that in my area it is a serious problem because for every person who is unemployed in Ontario there are more than two unemployed, in relation to population, in the province of Nova Scotia.
On the general subject of labour I also want to commend the government on its commitment made during the election campaign that a system of collective bargaining for civil servants will be established. I trust and I fully expect that this system of collective bargaining will also include the so-called prevailing rates employees, because in the past there have been many abuses with regard to the rights of prevailing rates employees and also, of course, of civil servants.
I will be particularly interested, Mr. Speaker, in seeing the pattern of collective bargaining which is outlined in subsequent government legislation and the type of arbitration which is to be implemented in the event that the bargaining parties fail to agree.

Mr. Speaker, I note by the clock that it is six o'clock.
At six o'clock the house took recess.

AFTER RECESS

The house resumed at 8 p.m.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before the dinner recess I spoke of the need for assistance by way of the revision of the freight rates applicable on goods transported through the ports of Halifax and other maritime ports to offset the new indirect subsidies being given to the St. Lawrence area by the building of the St. Lawrence seaway and the use of icebreakers in winter. I also complimented the administration upon the announced increases and other new benefits being given to the armed forces. I dealt with the question of collective bargaining for civil servants.
There is one other aspect of the speech from the throne upon which I should like to comment before returning to the question of the Atlantic development board. The subject to which I should like to refer is the expressed intention of the government to bring into effect the 12-mile fishing limit along the shores of our nation. The establishment of such a limit will end the disgraceful situation in which foreign fishermen are able to exploit the riches of our inshore fisheries, while Canadian fishermen are limited by the 12-mile rule. This is a measure, Mr. Speaker, which will bring great satisfaction to the fishermen of my area, and is a very important conservation measure for the north Atlantic fisheries in these days of ever increasing trawler activity.
I might say that during the last election campaign some hon. members on the other side of the house from the Nova Scotia area said that this 12-mile limit could not be unilaterally established without causing a very serious rift in our relations with the United States. I can only conclude that hon. members based these statements upon the established ability of the government of that day to get into trouble in the field of foreign relations. I think they also underestimate the capacity of the new administration to diplomatically negotiate a matter of this sort.
May I express the hope that the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Robichaud), whom I compliment upon his recent appointment, will soon find the opportunity to explore the desirability of expanding the present system of federally operated bait and ice stations. This is a service that is presently limited to Newfoundland, and is one of the services
The Address-Mr. Regan taken over by Canada at the time Newfoundland entered confederation. The expansion of this program to Nova Scotia and other areas would be extremely beneficial and would encourage our fishermen. It would also provide employment in our fishing villages and encourage those who would like to go into the fishery but have hesitated to do so because of the lack of these facilities.
If I may, Mr. Speaker, I should like for a moment to quote from this morning's edition of the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. I think there is a particularly illuminating and interesting editorial in that newspaper and I shall deal briefly with only one aspect of it concerning the increased use of the committees of this house. The Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) has already indicated that this will be forthcoming. I quote:
More use should be made of the standing committees.
All too often these are bypassed completely: instead, long and rambling discourses are given in the committee of the whole house. The external affairs committee, for example, did not meet once during the life of the last parliament.
If the government would send more of its important legislation to the standing committee, and prevent prolonged debate at the report stage, a considerable amount of duplicate discussion would be avoided.
I applaud this sentiment, Mr. Speaker, and I am pleased to see that there is an indication from the Prime Minister that this will be done.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I should like to return to the question of the Atlantic development board, a matter which is of great concern to the maritime provinces. As I indicated earlier in my remarks, there was disappointment at the time the Atlantic development board was appointed when the former administration made it only an advisory board and largely a duplicate of the work of APEC. Yesterday the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) indicated that he is opposed to the expansion of the Atlantic development board from five members to eleven members. I want to say that I feel the Leader of the Opposition is in error in this view, and that such expansion of the board could not help but be very beneficial, particularly in view of the fact that the five-man board as constituted does not contain any representative from labour. The board, as constituted by the previous administration, does not contain any representative of Acadian culture. Oh, it is true there is a gentleman by the name of Mr. Lalonde who lives in Moncton at the present time but I understand he is temporarily stationed in the maritimes and comes originally from Sherbrooke, Quebec. There are other areas and other aspects of the maritime economy

The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker which certainly should be represented on this board, particularly in view of the fact that the present chairman of the board is a comparative newcomer to the maritimes and to this country. Perhaps this might be an added reason for having a broader representation on this particular board. .
May I, then, as a new member in this house state my approval of the speech from the throne and my appreciation of the portions therein which directly affect my constituency? May I say that it is a privilege to be associated in this house with hon. members from all four parties?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday I thought I had completed anything that I had to say during the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne. During the course of my remarks I stated that I intended to deal with the defence problem at the appropriate time, which I considered would be the occasion when the motion to set up a committee on defence was being discussed. However, in view of the turn of events that occurred through the moving of the subamendment by the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), I find it necessary to speak again.
In view of some of the statements made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson), I propose to deal in general with the problem of defence so far as it relates to the question of nuclear weapons. I will also refer to the subamendment and give a general indication as to the reasons for the stand the official opposition intends to take upon the subamendment. We meet here at a time when the nations of NATO are gathered in ministerial council to discuss the present and future of that organization which is the bulwark of our defence and the only assurance of our survival. This is a matter I dealt with at length prior to the defeat of my government in early February, and what I shall do now is deal with some of the subsequent events, some of the changes of viewpoint which have come to light in the government of today in its discharge of the responsibilities of office.
I am sure all who heard the former minister of defence speak this afternoon were impressed by the cogency of the arguments advanced by him and by the manner in which he placed the facts before the house, as they are and were. What I intend to do is review in some detail the changes of viewpoint on the part of ministers of the government, something of the gyromancy displayed this afternoon by the Prime Minister, and the changes of viewpoint on the part of the Liberal party. Indeed in this matter, while they would endeavour to lead the house to believe that
their's has been the course of decision and definiteness, I doubt whether in the history of any parliament there has ever been seen such changes of viewpoint on the part of responsible members of the House of Commons, members in the Liberal party, as they have been blown about by the political winds, by special pressures, or even by visits across the border.
As to the last reference I intend to call as my witness the Minister of National Defence (Mr. Hellyer). He has given his reasons for that sudden change of front by the Liberal party when, on the 12th day of January last, at Scarborough, the party that had stood against nuclear arms suddenly did an about turn. Indeed, sir, the conversion of Saul en route to Damascus could not be compared with the complete change of viewpoint of the Liberal party.

The Pentagon estimates bombers will remain a prime threat for several years, but the growth of the Soviet missile force-with no indication of any large new increase in bomber production-has caused Pentagon planners to rush more effort on missile defences.

Conceived in the early 1950's and built at a cost of about $3,700,000,000, this network of giant electronic computers linked with huge radars was designed to detect approaching enemy bombers and alert interceptors and local missile forces-including Bomarcs-directing them into positions to destroy the enemy.

So he knew it. He cannot have it both ways. If he is right, he must have known since 1959 that there was a commitment. Yet, knowing there was a commitment, as he now says based on my remarks in the house at that time, he and those associated with him did everything they could in order to prevent Canada having nuclear weapons. They did not find this out in 1963. They did not find it when the light shone on the Prime Minister of today at Scarborough in January. They knew it from the time I spoke, they say, on February 20, 1959. I mentioned our stand at that time. I shall not quote it because it has already been quoted. I followed that stand throughout the years under repeated questioning from the opposition of that period. On January 18, 1960, I said:
Canada's stand might be summarized in this way: eventually Canadian forces may require nuclear weapons if those forces are to be kept effective. We cannot change the principle of United States ownership-they have taken a firm stand in this regard-but there shall be Canadian control of use in Canada. I want to make it absolutely clear that nuclear weapons will not be used by Canadian forces except as the Canadian government may decide and in the manner approved by the Canadian government. Canada retains its full freedom of choice and decision.
Then, later on, on February 9 of the same year I said:
I might add that if and when Canada does acquire nuclear weapons it would be in accordance with her own national policies and with our obligations under the North Atlantic treaty.
Then on July 4, 1960-I do not want to fill the record up except to show in this way the consistency of our stand-I said:
On the one hand we are desirous of attaining disarmament. On the other hand we have to discharge our responsibility of ensuring to the maximum degree the security of the Canadian people. In so far as the discussions are concerned the responsibility must necessarily be that of the Minister of National Defence whose officers meet with their corresponding numbers in the United States and place before them the stand taken by the Canadian government, which is of the essence of any possible agreement in the future, namely, that if and when-
Over and over again I have said this.
-the Canadian government should decide to equip its forces with nuclear weapons those weapons will be under Canadian control and would be used in Canada only as a result of a decision by the Canadian government.
Later on, on a number of occasions, the same question was raised. It was raised on November 30, 1960, when my answer was:

I simply say that the position of Canada is completely unchanged. We have made it perfectly clear that when and if nuclear weapons are acquired we shall not accept them unless we have joint control and there has been no suggestion at any time of any watering down or diminution of that stand.
I come, now, to September 20, 1961, when I said this:
As was made clear during the discussion of the defence estimate we have also equipment which will enable the use of defensive nuclear weapons should the government decide that these are required in the interest of national security ... The government does not wish any decision it may take in this matter to impede in any way the substantial progress which may be possible in disarmament or limitation on the spread of nuclear weapons to the independent control of countries not already having them.

But should it be decided in the light of Canadian armament needs and defence responsibilities that nuclear weapons are to be had at any time, joint control is of the essence of the stand we have taken.

We will negotiate with the United States so that, as I said earlier, in case of need nuclear warheads will be made readily available.
Never at any time was an undertaking to accept nuclear weapons made by the government of Canada, and this was made clear by the former secretary of state for external affairs.

Now we are being prepared for the introduction of atomic arms into Canada.
I thought there had been a commitment on the basis of what I said in 1959, but not so according to the minister of defence. He added:
The campaign to wear down the resistance in this house and in the country has begun. Speeches are being made by the Prime Minister and by the Minister of National Defence which lead us to believe that the introduction of these weapons is inevitable. The commander in chief of NORAD was brought to Toronto to make a speech which would frighten the Canadian people into submission.
Into submission to whom?
At this point, Mr. Chairman, I think I should raise the question of the propriety of the Canadian government asking General Kuter to come and make a speech designed to do the government's political chores.
I am not going to make a reference to some other visits that have taken place. The present minister added:
I think if the government has any policy in which it firmly believes, it should state the case and accept the responsibility without trying to palm it off on military officers.
We never tried to palm anything out on military officers, and we did not want to be palmed out either.
Then, as recorded at page 8231 of Hansard for September 12, 1961 the present minister said:
Under these circumstances our Bomarc, even if it had any utility whatsoever, and our defence mechanisms other than warning and reconnaissance do not in fact protect the deterrent. They may do other things, but they do not accomplish this end.
For this reason we continue to believe that it is not worth while to put Canada Into the atomic club.
That is what they meant by the atomic club, and they spoke against it. Then he said this:
-when the advantage of having atomic weapons on Canadian soil is so negligible. We reserve the right to reassess this position if at any time in the future the west should be successful in developing a really effective anti-missile missile.
You will pardon me, Mr. Speaker, if I refer again to the minister of defence. What did he say about the Bomarc? On October 31, 1960, speaking at Saint John he was reported in the Saint John Telegraph-Journal as follows:
The outspoken M.P. for Toronto-Trinity said, "the Bomarc missile is about the most useless expense of money you can devise. The government might as well collect taxes and dump the money into Northumberland strait."
Mr. Speaker, the instrument that would have made Canada the last few knots on the tail-the value of it-was not worth
The Address-Mr. Diefenbaker dumping into the Northumberland strait, according to the Minister of National Defence, but now it is to be equipped with nuclear warheads. Oh, how they ridiculed us. I ask why the change? I suppose we will never know, but the Minister of National Defence gives quite a viewpoint on the subject. When he was asked in Vancouver how this great change, this vast metamorphosis, came about, he said:
Lester Pearson advocated nuclear weapons for Canada because of new and vital information he received during the Cuban crisis. Paul Hellyer refused to say what the information was but he said Mr. Pearson realized he had to move immediately to save Canada's image within NATO and the United Nations.
What about the image of Canada in 1959 and 1960 and 1961, when the present Prime Minister, who had received the highest honour that could come to any Canadian internationally, the Nobel prize, who had occupied these high international positions, from day to day was castigating the government for daring to consider entering into an agreement that would have made possible the availability of nuclear weapons. The Vancouver report continues:
Hellyer said the Liberal leader was informed by private U.S. military and NATO sources that Canada's integrity had dropped to an all-time low.
Where would Canada's integrity have been if we had followed the advice of the opposition in 1959, 1960 and 1961?
"Washington was boiling," Hellyer said.
You can see the effervescence rise. "Washington was boiling"-boiling for what reason? Was it boiling because we dared to assert that in co-operation our sovereignty should be maintained. Referring to the Prime Minister the report continued:
He was continually asked "What's wrong with Canada?'' added Hellyer. Because of the grave situation Mr. Pearson felt Canada would have to take a positive stand in order to save her position of prestige.
I make no observation on that. Now, Mr. Speaker, I also want to read what the Minister of National Defence said. I have here an article written in the Toronto Telegram of September 20. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, that when they start turning author and writing articles, that is when difficulties arise. I point that out for the benefit of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon).

This article is headed, "The Bomarc debate". It is entitled "We shouldn't delude ourselves", by Paul Hellyer.
I agree with that. This is what he said:
Canada should not adopt defensive atomic weapons at this time, because none exist which provide any real protection.

The Address-Mr. Diejeribaker
What about the future? No one can foresee the future with clarity, but the position at present is pretty obvious in perspective.
October, November, December, January- less than four months later the perspective became clarified. Then he said:
After the Russians succeeded in building an atomic bomb they began-so it seemed at least- to build squadrons of long-range bombers capable of reaching targets on the North American continent. Realizing our vulnerability, we began a crash program of radar lines and interceptor construction.
The purpose of these-and it was never considered to be anything else by the military-was to provide protection for the U.S. strategic air command.
When I said that these things were not for the defence of Canada, they said I was wrong. But again I quote the Minister of National Defence in support of the position we took. Mr. Speaker, I was reading the approval of the Minister of National Defence. I know he has been kept by most important duties and I appreciate him now being in the house, because the vote is approaching. However, I was reading from an article written by him which should qualify him for membership in any authors' association for fiction. He also said this:
Any bombers shot down before reaching their targets would leave more of SAC intact and give more pilots a chance to return to their bases, from which they would deliver their retaliatory blow.
It was at this time-the early 1950's-that the concept of the Bomarc was accepted. A line of pilotless aircraft (Bomarc missiles) was planned to extend from coast to coast to provide increased protection for the atomic deterrent-the striking power of the United States air force.
The concept made some sense at the outset. It has long since been overtaken by time and technological development.
Well, Mr. Speaker, these were the viewpoints of last September, and now they are asking us to bring about this new plan whereby, as enunciated by the Prime Minister at Scarborough, they will bring over the atomic warheads, then they will place them on the Bomarcs, and then they will negotiate with the United States, to provide a dissolution after marriage. Why, Mr. Speaker, what nonsense is this?
Then the Minister of National Defence said, in this enlightening article:
October 1957 should be remembered as a turning point in modern military science. When the Russians put their first sputnik into orbit, and proved that they could easily build missiles capable of striking north Amercia, the missile age dramatically began. The subsequent five years have produced miracles in research and development.
Then he said:
Shorter range missiles can be fired from ships or submarines at sea. Air to ground missiles, otherwise known as stand-off bombs, can be carried under the wings of giant aircraft.
Against these three kinds of missiles there is, at the present time, no defence.
Now sir, I ask, what brought about the change of opinion? All I have tried to do this
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l
evening is simply review what has taken place. I have a great deal more material, equally effective, or revealing, I should say, that I will use on another occasion. No one yet knows the reason why on January 12 the Prime Minister announced a new policy. Why, it came with such revolting suddenness that the Manitoba Liberal association in session had just decided that they would not have nuclear weapons, and then they turned a complete somersault. They could not believe it. Possibly it will not be very long before we know some of the things that took place, some of the words of deep approval that were given to the Prime Minister for giving this remarkable calisthenic performance.
Sir, what is the policy today? Round and round it goes; what it is, nobody knows. Again I ask, what is it today? Well, on January 25 the Prime Minister stated in the House of Commons that they would accept a nuclear role at the moment. He intimated that this role would be changed if a Liberal government was in power. Cannot we just have some information. Was it arranged with the president at the siesta in Hyannis Port?

Was it arranged that if we would accept nuclear weapons, or if we would enter into an agreement such as was outlined today, there would then be a renegotiation so that Canada could renegotiate herself out of that agreement? Surely we are entitled to know. It is very obvious that we are not going to have the opportunity. Today the Secretary of State (Mr. Pickersgill), who is one of our leading authorities on constitutional development by appointment, said this: "You have the opportunity now to discuss it. We have not denied you that opportunity. One of the opposition parties has moved a subamendment, and we are going to let you discuss it". In effect, that is what he said. He said: "We have not denied you the right. Here you are; you can discuss it". That is not enough, Mr. Speaker. We have to know the reason for the change that has taken place in the attitude of this government over the stand which they took for three long years. Was that a conscientious stand which they took, or was it a political stand? Was the change, the migration from one side to the other in January, based on a consideration of the needs of Canadian security without regard to political considerations or was it determined as a result of representations made to the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) or to the minister of defence (Mr. Hellyer) by any one else at that time? These are questions whose answers we have a right to know.

I found it difficult to understand why the leader of the New Democratic party was unable to support the amendment which I moved. I felt it was one which deserved support, but the determination is always made on the basis of what is best for Canada and therefore I can make no criticism of that stand. I do not want to do anything which is detrimental to Canada but I am not going to be denied the right of having this important matter discussed and determined in parliament. The subject of nuclear arms is one upon which one's opinion changes or, at least, is affected by emotional considerations; but I cannot, in discharge of my responsibilities as Leader of the Opposition, allow this government to suggest to the opposition that because an opportunity has now come when the House of Commons may discuss this matter, that that is sufficient. Nothing of the kind. We want to know more. Whatever our views may be as to the need or the desirability of having the best defence which can be provided, parliament must have the right of decision. It will never have it. That was clear today.
I listened to the Prime Minister as he went over the field in a very able speech. How it would have appealed to me, that speech, if I had not known the facts as revealed by those quotations and many others which I could have placed before the house. We want to know. We want the facts. We cannot place reliance upon members of a government who in three years have held such a variety of opinions. What will the policy be? I think there were eight transitions between January 12 and the end of the campaign. Which of them represents the viewpoint of the members of the government today? We want the opportunity to be in committee-not the defence committee, but a committee of the House of Commons, here, to have this question answered. If hon. gentlemen opposite will not provide that, then let us have set aside a day on the basis of a resolution to be moved by the government in which frankly and fully the whole situation will be placed before parliament and the country. I cannot agree to less. At the moment I do not ask for more.
Yesterday the Prime Minister spoke of the Canadian people having decided all this. Well, 42 per cent, I think it was, voted in support of the government-43 per cent at the outside. Some 57 or 58 per cent voted otherwise. He said today this subject was one of the major issues. There has been no decision or mandate from the Canadian people in this regard. But whether with or without a mandate, members of parliament have their responsibility. All of us are prepared to have placed before us, not in panegyric form but in factual summary and analysis, the present 28902-5-10
The Address-Mr. Girouard situation. You will remember, sir, how those who now support this government poured their scorn on me when I said: Let us wait until the NATO meeting at which the whole question of defence will receive material consideration. They said: Nothing of the kind. Tomorrow and the next day the nations of NATO will determine one of the greatest questions facing the western world, namely, whether or not there is to be set up a multinational nuclear force and the terms upon which this would be done. Tremendous changes in defence thinking have taken place in the last few months. Britain had an agreement with the United States to have the Sky-bolt. That was changed as a result of the attitude taken by the United States, although Britain had depended upon it. Italy and Turkey had Jupiter missile bases upon which they depended. They are removed because of the changing concepts of defence. The new plan is, first, submarines and ships with Polaris missiles to be launched from them. The whole question of defence, as the minister of defence said so well last September, is changing and changeable. Therefore, I say that on the basis of the fact that we have had an undertaking, a statement, from the mover of this amendment that the problem is that parliament has not been consulted, believing that, as a result, it could be taken that these words are incorporated, namely "without consulting parliament", and that then the resolution would read in our interpretation-
-we regret that Your Excellency's advisers have indicated their intention without consulting parliament of acquiring nuclear arms for Canadian forces-
-we intend to support the subamendment. (Translation):

Mr. Speaker, I wish to thank the house for giving a member of each party the opportunity to put forward his views on what is going on in this chamber.
I noticed that the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) has tried to limit my loquaciousness by forcing me to reduce my speech to some four minutes.
I shall therefore gloss over the congratulations which I intended to offer and the suggestions which I was hoping to put forward in this house in the name of the voters of the riding of Labelle who, as you no doubt know, have always been proud of the fact that they elected Henri Bourassa in 1900.
The other day, as I was listening to the junior member for Lotbiniere (Mr. Choquette), I was wondering whether he would show as much courage as Henri Bourassa who, while still young, left the ranks of the Liberal party to sit as an independent member.

Division
Mr. Speaker, the Liberal party platform has been quite interesting for the voters during the last election campaign except in one respect, where there is a lot of discussion, and, this evening, it is incumbent upon me to define the policy of my party on nuclear arms.
I believe that the Liberal party has not gained by the last election. Everybody noticed that western Canada, not altogether reluctant to accept nuclear arms, has nevertheless supported a party which was against accepting them, while the province of Quebec, opposed to nuclear arms, has nevertheless been generous towards the party in power.
But I must admit that a few days only after the election, I shuddered when I noticed the haste with which the present Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and the minister of defence (Mr. Hellyer) undertook to acquire nuclear arms. It came about so fast that, today, the members in this house are wondering whether they shall grant their support to a government which has made commitments so hurriedly without even consulting the house.
As far as I am concerned, I must say in my capacity as representative of La Macaza, where a Bomarc missile base is located- quite a significant fact-that even the workers of La Macaza, who helped my election, gave me the definite responsibility of opposing all acquisition of nuclear arms.
